chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — London. An ante-chamber in the King’s palace
paragraphs: [Enter the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of Ely.]

CANTERBURY. My lord, I'll tell you—that same bill is being pushed again, the one that nearly passed against us in the eleventh year of the last king's reign. It would have gone through, except the unsettled and turbulent times shoved it aside.
ELY. But how, my lord, shall we resist it now?

CANTERBURY. It must be considered. If it passes against us, we lose more than half of what we own. They would strip from us all the secular lands that devout men have left to the Church by their wills. The valuation runs like this: enough to maintain, for the King's honor, a full fifteen earls, fifteen hundred knights, and six thousand two hundred good squires; and for the relief of lepers and the weak elderly—those poor faint souls past physical labor—a hundred well-supplied almshouses; and into the King's coffers besides, a thousand pounds a year. That's how the bill runs.
ELY. That would drink deep.
CANTERBURY. It would drink the cup and all.
ELY. But what's the way to prevent it?
CANTERBURY. The King is full of grace and fair judgment.
ELY. And a true lover of the holy Church.

CANTERBURY. The way he carried himself in his youth gave no sign of it. The breath had barely left his father's body when his wildness, mortified within him, seemed to die too. At that very moment, sober reflection came like an angel and whipped the offending Adam out of him, leaving his body a paradise to enclose and contain heavenly spirits. Never was a scholar made so suddenly; never did reform come flooding in with such a heady current scouring out faults; never did Hydra-headed wilfulness so quickly lose its seat—and all at once—as in this king.
ELY. We are blessed in the change.

CANTERBURY. Just hear him reason about theology, and full of admiration you'd inwardly wish the King had been made a prelate. Hear him debate matters of state, and you'd say that had been his entire study. Listen to him discuss war, and you'll hear a terrifying battle rendered in music. Turn him to any question of policy, and he'll untie its Gordian knot as easily as undoing his garter; so that when he speaks the air itself, that licensed wanderer, falls still, and silent wonder lurks in men's ears to catch his sweet and honeyed sentences. The practical art of living must have been the teacher of this theory—which is a wonder, since his Grace seemed to gather it from idle pursuits, with rough, unlettered, shallow company, his hours filled with riots, banquets, and sports. He was never noticed studying, never withdrawing, never separating himself from public haunts and the crowd.

ELY. The strawberry grows beneath the nettle, and wholesome berries thrive and ripen best beside fruit of lower quality. So the Prince concealed his contemplation behind a veil of wildness, which no doubt grew like summer grass—fastest at night, unseen, yet steadily increasing in his faculties.
CANTERBURY. It must be so, for miracles have ceased, and so we must accept the means by which things come to be perfected.
ELY. But, my good lord, what about easing this bill the Commons are pushing? Does his Majesty incline toward it, or not?

CANTERBURY. He seems undecided—or rather leaning more toward our side than favoring those who oppose us. I've made an offer to his Majesty, on behalf of our spiritual convocation and in regard to matters now in hand—which I've laid out for his Grace at length, concerning France—to give a greater sum than the clergy has ever at one time given to any of his predecessors.
ELY. How was this offer received, my lord?

CANTERBURY. With good acceptance from his Majesty—except that there wasn't time enough to hear, as I could see his Grace wished to, the particulars and clear lines of his true claims to certain dukedoms, and generally to the crown and throne of France, descending from Edward, his great-grandfather.
ELY. What was the interruption that broke this off?
CANTERBURY. The French ambassador asked for an audience at that very moment. And the hour, I think, has come to give him a hearing. Is it four o'clock?
ELY. It is.
CANTERBURY. Then let's go in, to learn his message—which I could readily guess at before the Frenchman speaks a word of it.
ELY. I'll attend you, and I'm eager to hear it.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — The same. The presence chamber
paragraphs: [Enter King Henry, Gloucester, Bedford, Clarence, Warwick, Westmorland, Exeter and Attendants.]
KING HENRY V. Where is my gracious Lord of Canterbury?
EXETER. Not present here.
KING HENRY V. Send for him, good uncle.
WESTMORLAND. Shall we call in the ambassador, my liege?
KING HENRY V. Not yet, cousin. Before we hear him, we want to be clear on some weighty matters concerning us and France.
[Enter the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of Ely.]
CANTERBURY. God and his angels guard your sacred throne, and make you long worthy of it!

KING HENRY V. We thank you. My learned lord, please proceed and explain, justly and conscientiously, why the Salic law they have in France should or should not bar us in our claim. And God forbid, my dear and faithful lord, that you should shape, twist, or bend your reading—or carefully burden your conscience by opening up false claims whose right does not stand in honest colors with the truth. For God knows how many men now in good health will shed their blood in confirmation of what your Reverence urges us to do. Therefore take heed how you stake our person, how you wake our sleeping sword of war. We charge you in the name of God: take heed. For never two such kingdoms went to war without much loss of blood, every guiltless drop of which is a sorrow and a sore complaint against the man whose wrongs put the edge on the swords that lay waste so much brief mortality. Speak under this solemn charge, my lord, for we will hear, note, and believe in our heart that whatever you say has been washed clean in your conscience, as pure as sin made clean by baptism.

CANTERBURY. Then hear me, gracious sovereign—and you peers, who owe yourselves, your lives, and your service to this imperial throne. There is no obstacle to your Highness's claim to France except this, which they cite from Pharamond: _In terram Salicam mulieres ne succedant_—"No woman shall succeed in Salic land." This Salic land the French unjustly gloss as the realm of France, and Pharamond as the founder of the law and of this bar against females. Yet their own historians faithfully affirm that the Salic land is in Germany, between the rivers Sala and Elbe. There Charlemagne, having subdued the Saxons, left certain French settlers behind. Disdaining the German women for some loose habits, they established this law: no female should inherit in Salic land. That Salic, as I said, between the Elbe and the Sala, is today in Germany called Meissen. So it's clear the Salic law was not devised for the realm of France; nor did the French even possess the Salic land until four hundred and twenty-one years after the death of King Pharamond, who is supposed—idly—to have founded this law. He died in the year of our redemption 426; and Charlemagne subdued the Saxons and settled the French beyond the river Sala in the year 805. Besides, their own writers say that King Pepin, who deposed Childeric, made his claim and title to the crown of France as heir general, being descended from Blithild, daughter of King Clothair. Hugh Capet too, who usurped the crown from Charles Duke of Lorraine—sole male heir of the true line and stock of Charlemagne—to give his title some show of truth (though in pure fact it was corrupt and worthless), traced himself as heir to Lady Lingare, daughter of Charlemain, who was the son of Lewis the Emperor, and Lewis the son of Charlemagne. King Lewis the Tenth too, sole heir to the usurper Capet, could not keep his conscience quiet wearing the crown of France until he was satisfied that the fair Queen Isabel, his grandmother, was lineal descendant of Lady Ermengare, daughter to Charles, the said Duke of Lorraine. By this marriage the line of Charlemagne was reunited to the crown of France. So that, as clear as the summer sun: King Pepin's title, Hugh Capet's claim, King Lewis's satisfaction—all rest on right and title through the female line. So do the kings of France, even to this day; though they would hold up this Salic law to bar your Highness from claiming through the female, and would rather hide themselves in a net than openly defend their crooked titles, usurped from you and your forefathers.
KING HENRY V. May I, with right and conscience, make this claim?

CANTERBURY. The sin upon my head, dread sovereign! For in the Book of Numbers it is written: "When the man dies, let the inheritance pass to his daughter." Gracious lord, stand for what is yours! Unfurl your bloody flag! Look back to your mighty ancestors! Go, my dread lord, to your great-grandfather's tomb, from whom you claim—invoke his warlike spirit, and your great-uncle's, Edward the Black Prince, who on French ground played a tragedy, defeating the full power of France while his mighty father stood smiling on a hill, watching his lion's whelp forage in the blood of French nobility. O noble English, who could engage the full pride of France with only half their forces and let the other half stand laughing by, all idle and cold for action!

ELY. Wake the memory of these valiant dead, and renew their feats with your powerful arm. You are their heir; you sit upon their throne. The blood and courage that made them famous runs in your veins. And my thrice-mighty liege is in the very May-morning of his youth—ripe for exploits and mighty enterprises.
EXETER. Your brother kings and monarchs of the earth all expect you to rouse yourself, as the earlier lions of your line did.

WESTMORLAND. They know your Grace has cause and means and might—as your Highness has. Never did a King of England have nobles richer or subjects more loyal, whose hearts have already left their bodies here in England and lie encamped in the fields of France.

CANTERBURY. O, let their bodies follow, my dear liege—with blood and sword and fire to win your right. In aid of which we of the spiritualty will raise your Highness such a mighty sum as the clergy never at one time gave to any of your ancestors.
KING HENRY V. We must not only arm to invade France but allocate forces to defend against the Scot, who will raid us at every opportunity.
CANTERBURY. The men of the border marches, gracious sovereign, will be wall enough to defend our inland from pilfering raiders.

KING HENRY V. We don't mean only the running snatchers, but fear the main intention of the Scots, who have always been a fickle neighbor to us. You'll read that my great-grandfather never went into France with his army but the Scot came pouring upon his undefended kingdom like the tide through a breach, with the full brim of his force, harrying the stripped land with hot attacks, ringing castles and towns with cruel sieges, so that England, empty of defense, shook and trembled at the bad neighborhood.

CANTERBURY. She has been more feared than harmed by it, my liege. Just consider her own example: when all her chivalry was in France and she a mourning widow without her nobles, she not only defended herself well but captured the King of Scots like a stray, and sent him to France to swell King Edward's fame with captive kings and make her chronicle as rich with praise as the seafloor is rich with sunken wreck and untold treasure.

WESTMORLAND. But there's an old and true saying: "If you would France win, then with Scotland first begin." For once the eagle England is out hunting, the weasel Scot comes sneaking to her unguarded nest and sucks her princely eggs, playing the mouse in the cat's absence—tearing up more than she can eat.

EXETER. It follows then that the cat must stay home. Yet that is only a strained necessity, since we have locks to safeguard valuables and clever traps to catch petty thieves. While the armed hand fights abroad, the prudent head defends itself at home. For government, divided into high, low, and lower parts, still keeps in one accord—coming together in a full and natural cadence, like music.

CANTERBURY. That's why heaven divides the state of man into various functions, setting endeavor in constant motion, with obedience fixed as its aim or target. So work the honeybees, creatures who teach an ordered kingdom how to function by natural rule. They have a king and officers of various kinds: some, like magistrates, correct at home; others, like merchants, venture trade abroad; others, like soldiers, armed with their stings, plunder the summer's velvet buds and bring the booty home in merry march to their emperor's royal tent. He, busy in his majesty, surveys the singing masons building roofs of gold, the orderly citizens kneading the honey, the poor porter-mechanics crowding their heavy burdens through his narrow gate, the sad-eyed justice with his surly hum delivering the lazy yawning drone to pale executioners. I draw this conclusion: many things, all answering to one common purpose, can work in different ways. As many arrows shot in different directions all reach one mark; as many roads converge on one town; as many fresh streams meet in one salt sea; as many lines close at the dial's center—so a thousand actions, once begun, end in one purpose and may all be well carried out without defeat. Therefore to France, my liege! Divide your happy England into four; take one quarter into France, and with that you shall make all of Gaul tremble. If we, with three times that force left at home, cannot defend our own doors from the dog, then let us be mauled, and let our nation lose the name for toughness and statecraft.
KING HENRY V. Call in the messengers sent from the Dauphin.
[Exeunt some Attendants.]

Now we are fully resolved. By God's help, and yours—the noble sinews of our power—we will bend France to our awe, or break it all to pieces. Either we'll sit there ruling in a wide empire over France and all her near-kingly dukedoms, or lay these bones in an unworthy urn, tombless, with no memorial over them. Either our history shall speak our deeds freely, with full voice—or else our grave, like a Turkish mute, will have a tongueless mouth, unworshipped, without even a wax epitaph.
[Enter Ambassadors of France.]
Now we are well prepared to hear the pleasure of our fair cousin the Dauphin. For we hear your greeting is from him, not from the King.
FIRST AMBASSADOR. May it please your Majesty to give us leave to deliver freely what we are charged with? Or shall we offer the Dauphin's meaning and our message only sparingly, at a distance?

KING HENRY V. We are no tyrant, but a Christian king, to whose grace our passions are as subject as the wretches fettered in our prisons. Therefore tell us the Dauphin's mind with frank and uncurbed plainness.

AMBASSADOR. Thus, then, in brief. Your Highness, having lately sent into France, claimed certain dukedoms by right of your great predecessor King Edward the Third. In answer to that claim, the prince our master says you taste too much of your youth, and warns you that there is nothing in France to be won with a nimble dance. You cannot revel your way into dukedoms there. Therefore he sends you something more suited to your spirit: this barrel of treasure. In exchange, he requests that the dukedoms you claim hear no more of you. This is what the Dauphin says.
KING HENRY V. What treasure, uncle?
EXETER. Tennis balls, my liege.

KING HENRY V. We are glad the Dauphin is so playful with us. We thank you for his present and for your pains. When we have matched our rackets to these balls, we will, by God's grace, play a set in France that shall strike his father's crown into the hazard. Tell him he has picked a quarrel with such a player that all the courts of France will be disturbed with our chases. We understand him well: how he throws our wilder days back at us, not weighing what use we made of them. We never valued this poor seat of England, and therefore, while living abroad in spirit, gave ourselves to barbarous licence—as it is always common that men are merriest when away from home. But tell the Dauphin I will keep my state, be like a king, and show my sail of greatness when I rouse myself on my throne of France. For that I have set aside my majesty and plodded like a workingman through working days; but I shall rise there with such full glory that I will dazzle every eye in France—yes, strike the Dauphin blind to look on us. And tell the merry prince this mock of his has turned his tennis balls into cannon stones, and his soul shall stand sorely charged for the wasteful vengeance that will fly with them. Many thousand widows shall this his mock mock out of their dear husbands, mock mothers from their sons, mock castles down. And some are not yet conceived or born who shall have cause to curse the Dauphin's scorn. But this all lies in the will of God, to whom I appeal; and in whose name tell the Dauphin I am coming to take revenge as I may, and to put forth my rightful hand in a well-sanctified cause. So be on your way in peace—and tell the Dauphin his jest will taste of shallow wit when thousands weep more than ever laughed at it. Escort them out safely.—Fare you well.
[Exeunt Ambassadors.]
EXETER. That was a merry message.

KING HENRY V. We hope to make the sender blush at it. Therefore, my lords, do not waste a fortunate hour that could advance our expedition. We have no thought now except France—save those thoughts to God that run before our business. Let our supplies for these wars be gathered quickly, and everything considered that may, with reasonable speed, add more feathers to our wings. For, with God leading, we'll chide this Dauphin at his father's door. Let every man bend his thought to bringing this fair action under way.
[Exeunt.]
[Flourish. Enter Chorus.]

CHORUS. Now all the youth of England is on fire, and silken idleness lies forgotten in the wardrobe. Now the armorers thrive, and thought of honor reigns alone in every man's heart. They sell the pasture to buy the horse, following the mirror of all Christian kings—with winged heels, like English Mercuries. For now Expectation sits in the air, hiding a sword from hilt to point with imperial crowns, crowns, and coronets, promised to Harry and his followers. The French, well-informed of this most dreadful preparation, shake in fear, and with pale statecraft seek to divert the English plans. O England, model of your inward greatness—a little body with a mighty heart—what could you do, that honor would do for you, if all your children were kind and loyal! But see your fault! France has found in you a nest of hollow hearts, which he fills with treacherous gold. Three corrupted men—one, Richard Earl of Cambridge; the second, Henry Lord Scroop of Masham; and the third, Sir Thomas Grey, knight of Northumberland—have, for the gold of France (O guilt indeed!), entered into a conspiracy with fearful France. And by their hands this grace of kings must die, if hell and treason keep their promises, before he takes ship for France, and in Southampton. Stretch your patience, and we'll digest the awkwardness of distance and force a play. The bribe is paid; the traitors agreed; the King is set out from London; and our scene is now carried, gentle audience, to Southampton. There is your playhouse now, there must you sit; and from there to France we shall convey you safe, and bring you back, charming the narrow seas to give you gentle passage. For if we can, we will not upset one stomach with our play. But, till the King appears—and not till then—we shift our scene to Southampton.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — London. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Corporal Nym and Lieutenant Bardolph.]
BARDOLPH. Well met, Corporal Nym.
NYM. Good morning, Lieutenant Bardolph.
BARDOLPH. So—are Ensign Pistol and you friends yet?

NYM. For my part, I don't care. I say little; but when the time comes, there'll be smiles—or whatever it turns out to be. I don't dare to fight, but I'll wink and keep my blade ready. It's a plain one, but so what? It will toast cheese, and it'll endure cold as well as another man's sword. And that's that.
BARDOLPH. I'll stand you a breakfast to make you friends; and all three of us will be sworn brothers off to France. Let it be so, good Corporal Nym.
NYM. Faith, I'll live as long as I can—that's the sure part. And when I can't live any longer, I'll do what I can. That's my position, that's the meeting point of it.
BARDOLPH. It's certain, corporal, that he's married to Nell Quickly; and she certainly did you wrong, since you were engaged to her.

NYM. I can't say. Things must be as they may. Men may sleep, and have their throats about them at that time; and they say knives have edges. It must be as it may. Though patience is a tired mare, still she'll plod on. There must be conclusions. Well, I can't say.
[Enter Pistol and Hostess.]
BARDOLPH. Here comes Ensign Pistol and his wife. Good Corporal, be patient now. How are you, mine host Pistol!
PISTOL. Lowly cur, do you call me "host"? Now, by this hand, I swear I scorn the term; nor shall my Nell keep lodgers.

HOSTESS. No, by my faith, not for long. For we can't lodge and board a dozen or fourteen gentlewomen who live honestly by their needlework without it being thought right away that we keep a brothel. [Nym and Pistol draw.] Oh, woe is the day, Lady—if he hasn't drawn now! We shall see willful adultery and murder committed.
BARDOLPH. Good Lieutenant! Good corporal! No fighting here.
NYM. Pah!
PISTOL. Pah to you, Iceland dog! You prick-eared mongrel of Iceland!
HOSTESS. Good Corporal Nym, show your valor and put up your sword.
NYM. Will you clear off? I'd have you _solus_—alone.

PISTOL. _Solus_, you outrageous dog! O vile viper! The _solus_ in your most marvelous face; the _solus_ in your teeth, and in your throat, and in your hateful lungs—yes, in your belly, by God—and, worst of all, within your nasty mouth! I throw the _solus_ back into your bowels; for I can take fire, and Pistol's hammer is cocked, and flashing fire will follow.

NYM. I am no demon; you cannot summon me with conjuring. I'm in the mood to thrash you reasonably well. If you turn foul with me, Pistol, I will scour you with my rapier, as I may, in fair terms. If you'd step aside, I'd prick your guts a little, in good terms, as I may—and that's the humor of it.
PISTOL. O vile braggart and damnable furious creature! The grave gapes wide, and doting death is near—therefore breathe out your last.
BARDOLPH. Hear me, hear what I say. Whichever of you strikes the first blow, I'll run him through to the hilt, as I am a soldier.
[Draws.]
PISTOL. An oath of mighty force—and fury shall abate. Give me your fist, your forefoot give me. Your spirits are most brave.
NYM. I will cut your throat one time or another, in fair terms: that is the humor of it.

PISTOL. "Couper la gorge"—cut the throat. That's the word. I defy you again. O hound of Crete, do you think to win my wife? No! Off to the hospital with you, and from the infamous sweating-tub fetch out the leprous kite of Cressid's kind—Doll Tearsheet by name—and marry her. I have, and I will hold, the former Quickly as my only one. And _pauca_—few words—there's enough. Move along.
[Enter the Boy.]

BOY. Mine host Pistol, you must come to my master, and you too, hostess. He is very sick and wants to go to bed. Good Bardolph, put your red face between his sheets and serve as a warming pan. Faith, he's very ill.
BARDOLPH. Away, you rogue!
HOSTESS. By my faith, he'll feed the crow as a pudding one of these days. The King has broken his heart. Good husband, come home right away.
[Exeunt Hostess and Boy.]
BARDOLPH. Come, shall I make you two friends? We must go to France together. Why the devil should we keep knives to cut one another's throats?
PISTOL. Let floods overflow, and fiends howl for food!
NYM. Will you pay me the eight shillings I won from you at betting?
PISTOL. The slave who pays is base.
NYM. I will have it now—that's the humor of it.
PISTOL. Let manhood decide it. Have at you.
[They draw.]
BARDOLPH. By this sword, whoever makes the first thrust, I'll kill him. By this sword, I will.
PISTOL. A sword is an oath, and oaths must have their course.
BARDOLPH. Corporal Nym, if you'll be friends, be friends; if you won't, then be enemies with me too. Please, put it up.
NYM. Will I have my eight shillings I won from you at betting?

PISTOL. A noble you shall have, and paid on the spot; and liquor too I'll give you, and friendship and brotherhood shall be joined. I'll live by Nym, and Nym shall live by me. Isn't that fair? For I shall be a sutler with the army, and profits will come in. Give me your hand.
NYM. I shall have my noble?
PISTOL. Paid in cash, most justly.
NYM. Well, then, that's the humor of it.
[Enter Hostess.]
HOSTESS. As you ever came of women, come quickly to Sir John. Ah, poor heart! He is so shaken with a burning fever that it's pitiful to see. Sweet men, come to him.
NYM. The King has worked bad humors on the knight—that's the truth of it.
PISTOL. Nym, you've spoken right. His heart is fractured and shattered.
NYM. The King is a good king; but it must be as it may; he has his moods and his swings.
PISTOL. Let us mourn for the knight; for, little lambs, we will live on.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — Southampton. A council-chamber
paragraphs: [Enter Exeter, Bedford and Westmorland.]
BEDFORD. Before God, his Grace is bold to trust these traitors.
EXETER. They shall be arrested shortly.
WESTMORLAND. How smooth and even they carry themselves! As if allegiance sat in their hearts, crowned with faith and constant loyalty.
BEDFORD. The King has been informed of everything they intend, through an interception they don't dream of.
EXETER. Indeed—but that the man who was his bedfellow, whom he has dulled and surfeited with gracious favors, that he should sell his sovereign's life to death and treachery for a foreign purse!
[Trumpets sound. Enter King Henry, Scroop, Cambridge and Grey.]

KING HENRY V. Now the wind sits fair, and we'll go aboard. My Lord of Cambridge, my kind Lord of Masham, and you, my gentle knight—give me your thoughts. Don't you think the forces we carry with us will cut their passage through the power of France, accomplishing the action for which we have assembled them?
SCROOP. No doubt, my liege, if every man does his best.

KING HENRY V. I don't doubt that, since we are well persuaded we don't carry a heart with us from here that doesn't grow in fair accord with ours; nor do we leave one behind that doesn't wish success and conquest to attend us.
CAMBRIDGE. Never was a monarch better feared and loved than your Majesty. There's not, I think, a subject who sits in heart-grief or unease under the sweet shade of your government.
GREY. True. Those who were your father's enemies have steeped their bile in honey and now serve you with hearts re-made of duty and zeal.
KING HENRY V. We therefore have great cause for thankfulness, and shall forget the use of our own hand sooner than the repayment of merit according to its weight and worthiness.
SCROOP. So service shall labor with steeled sinews, and labor shall refresh itself with hope, to do your Grace incessant services.

KING HENRY V. We judge no less. Uncle of Exeter, release the man committed yesterday who railed against our person. We consider it was excess of wine that set him on, and on further reflection we pardon him.
SCROOP. That is mercy, but too much leniency. Let him be punished, sovereign, lest your toleration set an example that breeds more of the same kind.
KING HENRY V. O, let us yet be merciful.
CAMBRIDGE. So may your Highness—and yet punish too.
GREY. Sir, you show great mercy if you give him life after a taste of severe correction.

KING HENRY V. Alas, your too-great love and care of me are heavy prayers against this poor wretch! If little faults, born of intemperance, are not to be winked at, how shall we open our eyes wide enough when capital crimes—chewed, swallowed, and digested—appear before us? We will still release that man, though Cambridge, Scroop, and Grey, in their dear care and tender preservation of our person, would have him punished. And now to our French business. Who are the latest commissioners?
CAMBRIDGE. I am one, my lord. Your Highness asked me to apply for it today.
SCROOP. So you did me, my liege.
GREY. And me, my royal sovereign.

KING HENRY V. Then, Richard Earl of Cambridge, there is yours; there yours, Lord Scroop of Masham; and, sir knight Grey of Northumberland, this is yours. Read them, and know that I know your worthiness. My Lord of Westmorland, and uncle Exeter, we go aboard tonight.—Why, how now, gentlemen! What do you see in those papers that you lose so much color?—Look how they change! Their cheeks are pale as paper.—Why, what is in there that has so cowed your blood and chased it from your faces?
CAMBRIDGE. I confess my fault, and submit myself to your Highness's mercy.
GREY, SCROOP. To which we all appeal.

KING HENRY V. The mercy that was alive in me just now has been suppressed and killed by your own counsel. You must not dare, for shame, to speak of mercy—for your own reasons turn back into your hearts like dogs upon their masters, worrying you. See, my princes and my noble peers, these English monsters! My Lord of Cambridge here—you know how ready our love was to grant him everything befitting his honor; and this man, for a few light crowns, has lightly conspired and sworn himself to French plots to kill us here in Hampton. To the same plot this knight, no less bound to us in generosity than Cambridge, has also sworn. But, O—what shall I say to you, Lord Scroop? You cruel, ungrateful, savage, inhuman creature! You who carried the key to all my counsels, who knew the very bottom of my soul, who might almost have coined me into gold for your own use—is it possible that foreign hire could extract from you one spark of evil that might harm my finger? It is so strange that, though the truth of it stands out as plain as black on white, my eye can scarcely see it. Treason and murder always kept together, like two yoked devils sworn to each other's purpose, working so grossly toward a natural end that astonishment never even gasped at them. But you, against all proportion, brought wonder in to attend on treason and murder. Whatever cunning fiend it was that worked on you so monstrously has won the prize in hell for excellence; other devils that tempt to treason patch and bungle up damnation with rags, colors, and forms borrowed from glittering shows of piety. But the fiend that shaped you bade you simply stand up—gave you no excuse for committing treason, except to call you traitor. If the same demon who has fooled you should walk the world with his lion's stride, he might return to vast Tartarus and tell the legions, "I can never win a soul as easy as that Englishman's." O, how you have infected the sweetness of trust with suspicion! Do men show themselves dutiful? Why, so did you. Do they seem grave and learned? So did you. Are they of noble family? So were you. Do they seem religious? So did you. Or are they sparing in diet, free from coarse passion in either mirth or anger, constant in spirit, not swayed by the blood, dressed and finished in modest grace, not relying on the eye without the ear, and trusting neither except in purified judgment? Such, and so finely sifted, you seemed. And so your fall has left a kind of stain to mark out even the fullest-fraught and best-endowed man with some suspicion. I will weep for you. For this betrayal of yours, I think, is like another fall of man. Their crimes are now open. Arrest them to answer to the law; and may God acquit them of their plotting!

EXETER. I arrest you for high treason, by the name of Richard Earl of Cambridge. I arrest you for high treason, by the name of Henry Lord Scroop of Masham. I arrest you for high treason, by the name of Thomas Grey, knight, of Northumberland.
SCROOP. Our purposes God has justly discovered, and I repent my fault more than my death, which I beseech your Highness to forgive, though my body pay the price of it.

CAMBRIDGE. For me, the gold of France was not the seducer, although I admitted it as a motive to bring about more quickly what I intended. But thanks be to God for the prevention, in which I will heartily rejoice as I suffer, beseeching God and you to pardon me.

GREY. Never did a faithful subject rejoice more at the discovery of dangerous treason than I do at this moment, glad of myself for being prevented from a damned enterprise. Pardon my fault, sovereign, though not my body.

KING HENRY V. May God absolve you in his mercy! Hear your sentence. You have conspired against our royal person, joined with a declared enemy, and from his coffers received the golden earnest-money of our death. By it you would have sold your king to slaughter, his princes and peers to servitude, his subjects to oppression and contempt, and his whole kingdom to desolation. As for our own person, we seek no revenge. But we must so tend to the safety of our kingdom—whose ruin you have sought—that we deliver you to her laws. Therefore go your way, poor miserable wretches, to your death; may God in his mercy give you patience to endure its taste, and true repentance of all your dear offenses! Take them away.
[Exeunt Cambridge, Scroop and Grey, guarded.]

Now, lords, for France—the enterprise of which shall be as glorious to you as to us. We do not doubt a fair and lucky war, since God has so graciously brought to light this dangerous treason lurking in our path to hinder our beginnings. We do not doubt now but every obstacle is smoothed in our way. Then forth, dear countrymen! Let us deliver our strength into the hand of God, and put it straight into action. Cheerly to sea! Let the standards of war advance! No king of England, if not king of France!
[Flourish. Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — London. Before a tavern
paragraphs: [Enter Pistol, Nym, Bardolph, Boy and Hostess.]
HOSTESS. Please, honey, sweet husband, let me bring you as far as Staines.
PISTOL. No; for my manly heart aches. Bardolph, be cheerful; Nym, rouse your boasting veins; Boy, bristle up your courage. For Falstaff is dead, and we must grieve.
BARDOLPH. I wish I were with him, wherever he is—in heaven or in hell!

HOSTESS. No, surely he's not in hell. He's in Arthur's bosom, if ever any man went to Arthur's bosom. He made a finer end and went away as if he'd been any baptized child. He passed away just between twelve and one, just at the turning of the tide. After I saw him fumble with the sheets, and play with flowers, and smile at his fingertips, I knew there was only one way it could go. For his nose was as sharp as a pen, and he babbled of green fields. "How now, Sir John!" said I; "what, man! Be of good cheer." So he cried out, "God, God, God!" three or four times. Now I, to comfort him, told him he shouldn't think of God—I hoped there was no need for him to trouble himself with such thoughts yet. So he asked me to put more clothes on his feet. I put my hand into the bed and felt them, and they were as cold as any stone. Then I felt his knees, and so upward and upward, and all was as cold as any stone.
NYM. They say he cried out against sack-wine.
HOSTESS. Yes, that he did.
BARDOLPH. And against women.
HOSTESS. No, that he did not.
BOY. Yes, that he did; and said they were devils incarnate.
HOSTESS. He could never bear carnation—it was a color he never liked.
BOY. He said once that the devil would have him for his womanizing.
HOSTESS. He did, in a way, indeed handle women; but at the time he was feverish, and talking about the whore of Babylon.
BOY. Don't you remember—he saw a flea stuck on Bardolph's nose, and said it was a black soul burning in hellfire?
BARDOLPH. Well, the fuel that fed that fire is gone. That's all the wealth I got from his service.
NYM. Shall we move on? The King will be gone from Southampton.

PISTOL. Come, let's away. My love, give me your lips. Look after my goods and my belongings. Let common sense rule; the motto is "Cash on Delivery." Trust no one. For oaths are straws, men's faiths are wafer-cakes, and "Hold Fast" is the only true dog, my dear. Therefore, let _Caveto_—"Beware"—be your counselor. Go, clear your tear-filled eyes. Comrades in arms, let's to France—like horse-leeches, my boys, to suck, to suck, the very blood to suck!
BOY. And that's unwholesome food, they say.
PISTOL. Touch her soft mouth, and march on.
BARDOLPH. Farewell, hostess.
[Kissing her.]
NYM. I can't kiss—that is the humor of it. But, adieu.
PISTOL. Show your housewifery. Stay close inside, I command you.
HOSTESS. Farewell; adieu.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — France. The King’s palace
paragraphs: [Flourish. Enter the French King, the Dauphin, the Dukes of Berry and Brittany, the Constable and others.]

FRENCH KING. Thus comes the English upon us with full force, and it concerns us, more than carefully, to respond royally with our defenses. Therefore the Dukes of Berry and Brittany, of Brabant and Orleans, shall set out; and you, Prince Dauphin, with all swift dispatch, shall reinforce and renew our fortified towns with men of courage and the means to defend. For England's advance is as fierce as waters drawn into a whirlpool. So it suits us to be as cautious as fear may teach us, from recent examples left by the fatal and underestimated English upon our fields.

DAUPHIN. My most dreaded father, it is most fitting that we arm against the foe. For peace itself should not so dull a kingdom—even with no war or known quarrel in question—that defenses, musters, and preparations should not be kept up, assembled, and gathered as if war were imminent. Therefore, I say, it is fitting we all go out to inspect the sick and feeble parts of France. And let us do it with no display of fear—no, no more than if we heard England were busy with a Whitsun morris-dance. For, my good liege, she is so idly kinged, her scepter so foolishly carried by a vain, giddy, shallow, moody youth, that fear has no business with her.

CONSTABLE. O peace, Prince Dauphin! You are far too mistaken about this king. Ask your Grace the recent ambassadors with what great composure he heard their embassy, how well supplied with noble counselors, how modest in objection, and at the same time how terrible in steady resolution. You'll find his earlier vanities were only the outward show of a Roman Brutus, hiding discretion under a coat of folly—as gardeners hide with manure those roots that will first spring up and prove most delicate.

DAUPHIN. Well, it isn't so, my Lord High Constable. But even if we think it is, it doesn't matter. In matters of defense it's best to estimate the enemy as mightier than he seems, so the proper measures get taken. Otherwise, a weak and stingy estimate, like a miser, spoils its own coat by skimping on a little cloth.

FRENCH KING. Think of King Harry as strong; and, Princes, see that you strongly arm to meet him. His kindred have already feasted on us. He's bred from that bloody stock that haunted us along our familiar paths. Witness our too-memorable shame when the battle of Cressy was fatally struck, and all our princes were taken prisoner by the hand of that black name, Edward, Black Prince of Wales—while his mountain-tall father stood on a mountain, up in the air, crowned with the golden sun, watched his heroic offspring, and smiled to see him mangle the work of nature and deface the patterns that, by God and by French fathers, had been twenty years in the making. This is a shoot from that victorious stock; and let us fear his inborn might and destiny.
[Enter a Messenger.]
MESSENGER. Ambassadors from Harry King of England request admittance to your Majesty.
FRENCH KING. We'll give them an immediate audience. Go and bring them.
[Exeunt Messenger and certain Lords.]
You see this chase is hotly pursued, friends.

DAUPHIN. Turn and face them and stop the pursuit. Coward dogs bark loudest when what they seem to threaten runs far ahead of them. My good sovereign, take the English up short, and let them know what kind of monarchy you head. Self-love, my liege, is not so vile a sin as self-neglect.
[Enter Exeter.]
FRENCH KING. From our brother of England?

EXETER. From him. And he greets your Majesty thus: he requires you, in the name of God Almighty, to divest yourself, and lay aside the borrowed glories that, by gift of heaven and by the law of nature and of nations, belong to him and to his heirs—namely, the crown and all the wide-stretching honors that, by custom and the ordinance of time, belong to the crown of France. That you may know it's no sinister or awkward claim, picked from the wormholes of long-vanished days, nor raked from the dust of old oblivion, he sends you this most memorable lineage, truly demonstrative in every branch. He bids you look over this pedigree; and when you find him directly descended from his most famous of famous ancestors, Edward the Third, he bids you then resign your crown and kingdom, which you hold indirectly from him, the native and true claimant.
FRENCH KING. Or else what follows?

EXETER. Bloody force. For if you hide the crown even in your hearts, he will rake there for it. Therefore in fierce tempest he is coming, in thunder and in earthquake, like a Jove—so that if request fails, he will compel. And he bids you, in the name of the bowels of the Lord, hand over the crown, and take pity on the poor souls for whom this hungry war opens its vast jaws. And on your head he turns the widows' tears, the orphans' cries, the dead men's blood, the pining maidens' groans for husbands, fathers, and betrothed lovers, that shall be swallowed up in this quarrel. This is his claim, his threatening, and my message—unless the Dauphin is present here, to whom I bring greeting expressly as well.
FRENCH KING. For our part, we will consider this further. Tomorrow you shall carry our full intent back to our brother of England.
DAUPHIN. As for the Dauphin, I stand here for him. What is there from England to him?

EXETER. Scorn and defiance. Slight regard, contempt, and anything that won't disgrace the mighty sender—that's what he values you at. My king says this: if your father's Highness does not, by granting all his demands in full, sweeten the bitter mock you sent his Majesty, he'll call you to so hot an answer for it that the caves and womb-like vaults of France shall chide your trespass and echo back your mockery in the second-note thunder of his cannon.

DAUPHIN. Tell him: if my father returns a fair answer, it is against my will. For I desire nothing but war with England. To that end, suited to his youth and vanity, I sent him the Paris tennis balls.

EXETER. He'll make your Paris Louvre shake for it, were it the mistress-court of all mighty Europe. And be assured, you'll find a difference—as we, his subjects, have wondrously found—between the promise of his greener days and the man he masters now. Now he weighs time even to the last grain. You'll read that in your own losses, if he stays in France.
FRENCH KING. Tomorrow you shall know our mind in full.
[Flourish.]
EXETER. Dispatch us with all speed, lest our king come here himself to question our delay. For he has already set foot in this land.
FRENCH KING. You shall be dispatched soon with fair terms. A night is little breath and little pause to answer matters of such consequence.
[Exeunt.]
[Flourish. Enter Chorus.]

CHORUS. Thus with imagined wings our swift scene flies, in motion no less speedy than thought. Suppose that you have seen the well-equipped king at Hampton pier embark his royalty, and his brave fleet with silken streamers fanning the young sun. Play with your fancies, and in them behold ship-boys climbing on the hempen rigging; hear the shrill whistle that brings order to confused noise; behold the canvas sails, borne by the invisible creeping wind, draw the huge hulls through the furrowed sea, breasting the lofty surge. O, just imagine you stand on the shore and behold a city dancing on the unsteady waves—for so appears this majestic fleet, holding its true course to Harfleur. Follow, follow! Grapple your minds to the stern of this navy, and leave your England, still as dead midnight, guarded only by grandfathers, babies, and old women—either past or not yet come to full strength and vigor. For who is the man, with his chin just touched by one visible hair, who will not follow these select and choice-drawn cavaliers to France? Work, work your thoughts, and in them see a siege. Behold the cannon on their carriages, with fatal mouths gaping at girded Harfleur. Suppose the ambassador from the French comes back and tells Harry that the King offers him Katherine his daughter, and with her as dowry some petty and unprofitable dukedoms. The offer doesn't please; and the nimble gunner now touches the devilish cannon with his linstock,
[Alarum, and chambers go off.]
And down goes all before them. Still be kind, and fill out our performance with your mind.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — France. Before Harfleur
paragraphs: [Alarum. Enter King Henry, Exeter, Bedford, Gloucester and Soldiers, with scaling-ladders.]

KING HENRY V. Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more—or close the wall up with our English dead. In peace there's nothing that suits a man so well as modest stillness and humility. But when the blast of war blows in our ears, then imitate the action of the tiger: stiffen the sinews, summon up the blood, disguise fair nature with hard-featured rage. Then lend the eye a terrible aspect; let it pry through the gun-port of the head like the brass cannon; let the brow overhang it as fearfully as a weather-worn rock overhangs and juts above its battered base, washed by the wild and wasteful ocean. Now set the teeth and stretch the nostril wide, hold hard the breath, and bend every spirit up to its full height. On, on, you noblest English, whose blood is fetched from fathers war-proven! Fathers that, like so many Alexanders, have in these parts fought from morning till evening and sheathed their swords for lack of opponents. Don't dishonor your mothers; now prove that those you called fathers really did beget you. Be a pattern now to men of coarser blood, and teach them how to make war. And you, good yeomen, whose limbs were made in England, show us here the mettle of your pasture. Let us swear you are worth your breeding—which I do not doubt, for there is none among you so lowly and base that does not have a noble luster in his eyes. I see you stand like greyhounds in the slips, straining at the start. The game's afoot! Follow your spirit, and upon this charge cry, "God for Harry! England and Saint George!"
[Exeunt. Alarum, and chambers go off.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — The same
paragraphs: [Enter Nym, Bardolph, Pistol and Boy.]
BARDOLPH. On, on, on, on, on! To the breach, to the breach!
NYM. Please, corporal, stop. The blows are too hot; and for my own part, I haven't a spare set of lives. The humor of it is too hot—that's the very plain truth.
PISTOL. The plain truth is well said, for tempers are running high. Blows come and go; God's vassals drop and die. And sword and shield, in bloody field, win immortal fame.
BOY. I wish I were in an alehouse in London! I'd give all my fame for a pot of ale and safety.
PISTOL. And I. If wishes would do it for me, my plans would not fail me—and there I would speed.
BOY. As reliably—but not as truly—as the bird does sing on the bough.
[Enter Fluellen.]
FLUELLEN. Up to the breach, you dogs! Get going, you cowards!
[Driving them forward.]
PISTOL. Be merciful, great Duke, to men of mortal clay. Slow your rage, slow your manly rage, slow your rage, great Duke! Good fellow, slow your rage; show some mercy, sweet chick!
NYM. These are fine tempers! Your honor wins yourself bad humors.
[Exeunt all but Boy.]

BOY. Young as I am, I have observed these three swaggerers. I am servant-boy to all three of them; but all three of them together, if they tried to serve me, couldn't make one man. For indeed three such buffoons don't add up to a man. As for Bardolph, he's white-livered and red-faced; by which means he bluffs but doesn't fight. As for Pistol, he has a killing tongue and a quiet sword; by which means he breaks words and keeps weapons whole. As for Nym, he's heard that men of few words are the best men; and therefore he scorns to say his prayers, in case he should be thought a coward. But his few bad words are matched with as few good deeds; for he never broke any man's head but his own, and that was against a post when he was drunk. They'll steal anything and call it "purchase." Bardolph stole a lute-case, carried it twelve leagues, and sold it for three halfpence. Nym and Bardolph are sworn brothers in pilfering; in Calais they stole a fire-shovel. I knew by that piece of service that the men would carry coal. They want me to be as familiar with men's pockets as with their gloves or handkerchiefs—which much offends my manhood, if I were to take from another's pocket to put into mine; for it is plain pocketing up of wrongs. I must leave them and seek better service. Their villainy turns my weak stomach, so I must throw it up.
[Exit.]
[Enter Gower and Fluellen.]
GOWER. Captain Fluellen, you must come at once to the mines. The Duke of Gloucester wants to speak with you.

FLUELLEN. To the mines! Tell you the Duke, it is not so good to come to the mines. For, look you, the mines are not according to the disciplines of war. The hollows of them are not sufficient; for, look you, the adversary, you may explain to the Duke, has dug himself four yards under the counter-mines. By Jesu, I think he will blow up everything, if there are not better orders.
GOWER. The Duke of Gloucester, who has been given command of the siege, is being entirely directed by an Irishman—a very valiant gentleman, i'faith.
FLUELLEN. It is Captain Macmorris, is it not?
GOWER. I think it is.

FLUELLEN. By Jesu, he is as great an ass as any in the world. I will say as much to his beard. He has no more grasp of the true disciplines of war, look you, of the Roman disciplines, than has a puppy-dog.
[Enter Macmorris and Captain Jamy.]
GOWER. Here he comes; and the Scots captain, Captain Jamy, with him.

FLUELLEN. Captain Jamy is a marvelous valorous gentleman, that is certain; and of great quickness and knowledge in the ancient wars, upon my particular knowledge of his orders. By Jesu, he will maintain his argument as well as any military man in the world, in the disciplines of the pristine wars of the Romans.
JAMY. I say good day, Captain Fluellen.
FLUELLEN. Good-day to your worship, good Captain James.
GOWER. How now, Captain Macmorris! Have you given up on the mines? Have the sappers stopped?

MACMORRIS. By Christ, indeed! It is ill done! The work is given over, the trumpet sounds the retreat. By my hand I swear, and by my father's soul, the work is ill done; it is given over. I would have blown up the town, so Christ save me, indeed, in an hour. O, it is ill done, it is ill done; by my hand, it is ill done!

FLUELLEN. Captain Macmorris, I beseech you now—will you vouchsafe me, look you, a few disputations with you, partly touching or concerning the disciplines of the war, the Roman wars, in the way of argument, look you, and friendly communication; partly to satisfy my own opinion, and partly for the satisfaction, look you, of my mind, regarding the direction of military discipline. That is the point.
JAMY. It shall be very good, good faith, good captains both—and I shall return the favor with your good leave, as I may pick the occasion. That I shall, by Mary.

MACMORRIS. It is no time to discuss, so Christ save me. The day is hot, and the weather, and the wars, and the King, and the Dukes. It is no time to discuss. The town is besieged, and the trumpet calls us to the breach—and we are talking, and, by Christ, doing nothing. It is shame for us all. So God save me, it is shame to stand still. It is shame, by my hand. There are throats to be cut and work to be done—and nothing is being done, so Christ save me, indeed!

JAMY. By the mass, before these eyes of mine take themselves to slumber, I'll do good service, or I'll lie in the ground for it—aye, or go to death; and I'll repay it as valorously as I may, that I shall surely do, that is the long and the short of it. By Mary, I would very gladly have heard some discussion between you two.
FLUELLEN. Captain Macmorris, I think, look you, under your correction, there are not many of your nation—
MACMORRIS. Of my nation! What is my nation? Is it a villain, and a bastard, and a knave, and a rascal? What is my nation? Who talks of my nation?

FLUELLEN. Look you, if you take the matter otherwise than is meant, Captain Macmorris, perhaps I shall think you do not use me with that affability as, in discretion, you ought to use me, look you—being as good a man as yourself, both in the disciplines of war, and in the derivation of my birth, and in other particulars.
MACMORRIS. I do not know you to be so good a man as myself. So Christ save me, I will cut off your head.
GOWER. Gentlemen, both of you—you will mistake each other.
JAMY. Ah! That's a foul fault.
[A parley sounded.]
GOWER. The town sounds a parley.
FLUELLEN. Captain Macmorris, when there is a better opportunity to be required, look you, I will be so bold as to tell you I know the disciplines of war—and there is an end.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — Before the gates
paragraphs: [The Governor and some citizens on the walls; the English forces below. Enter King Henry and his train.]

KING HENRY V. How does the governor of the town resolve now? This is the last parley we'll allow. Therefore yield yourselves to our best mercy, or, like men proud of destruction, defy us to our worst. For, as I am a soldier—a name that in my thoughts suits me best—if I begin the bombardment once again, I will not leave the half-conquered Harfleur till in her ashes she lies buried. The gates of mercy shall all be shut up, and the blood-hardened soldier, rough and hard of heart, will range with bloody hand in full liberty, conscience wide as hell, mowing down like grass your fresh fair virgins and your flowering infants. What is it then to me if impious War, arrayed in flames like the prince of fiends, performs with his smirched complexion all cruel deeds linked to waste and desolation? What is it to me, when you yourselves are the cause, if your pure maidens fall into the hands of hot and forcing violation? What rein can hold licentious wickedness when he runs his fierce career down the hill? We might as fruitlessly waste our vain command upon the enraged soldiers as they pillage, as send orders to the leviathan to come ashore. Therefore, men of Harfleur, take pity on your town and your people, while my soldiers are yet under my command, while the cool and temperate wind of grace still blows away the filthy and contagious clouds of heady murder, plunder, and villainy. If not, in a moment look to see the blind and bloody soldier with foul hand defile the locks of your shrill-shrieking daughters; your fathers taken by their silver beards and their most reverend heads dashed against the walls; your naked infants impaled on pikes, while the mad mothers with their confused howls break open the clouds, as did the wives of Jewry at Herod's bloody-hunting slaughtermen. What do you say? Will you yield, and avoid this—or, guilty in your defense, be destroyed thus?

GOVERNOR. Our expectation comes to an end today. The Dauphin, of whom we entreated relief, returns us word that his forces are not yet ready to raise so great a siege. Therefore, great King, we yield our town and our lives to your soft mercy. Enter our gates; dispose of us and ours; for we can no longer defend ourselves.

KING HENRY V. Open your gates. Come, uncle Exeter—go and enter Harfleur; remain there, and fortify it strongly against the French. Show mercy to them all. For us, dear uncle, with winter coming on and sickness growing among our soldiers, we will retire to Calais. Tonight in Harfleur we shall be your guest; tomorrow we are set for the march.
[Flourish. The King and his train enter the town.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 4 — The French King’s palace
paragraphs: [Enter Katherine and Alice, an old Gentlewoman.]
KATHERINE. _Alice, you have been in England, and you speak the language well._
ALICE. _A little, madame._
KATHERINE. _Please, teach me; I must learn to speak it. What do you call_ la main _—the hand—in English?_
ALICE. _The hand? It is called_ de hand.
KATHERINE. De hand. _And the fingers?_
ALICE. _The fingers? By my faith, I forget the fingers; but I shall remember. The fingers? I think they are called_ de fingres; _yes_, de fingres.
KATHERINE. _The hand_, de hand; _the fingers_, de fingres. _I think I am a good student; I have gained two words of English quickly. What do you call the fingernails?_
ALICE. _The fingernails? We call them_ de nails.
KATHERINE. De nails. _Listen; tell me if I say it well:_ de hand, de fingres, _and_ de nails.
ALICE. _That is well said, madame; it is very good English._
KATHERINE. _Tell me the English for the arm._
ALICE. De arm, _madame._
KATHERINE. _And the elbow?_
ALICE. D'elbow.
KATHERINE. D'elbow. _I shall repeat to myself all the words you have taught me up to now._
ALICE. _It is too difficult, madame, I think._
KATHERINE. _Pardon me, Alice. Listen:_ d'hand, de fingres, de nails, d'arm, de bilbow.
ALICE. D'elbow, _madame._
KATHERINE. _O Lord God, I forget myself!_ D'elbow. _What do you call the neck?_
ALICE. De nick, _madame._
KATHERINE. De nick. _And the chin?_
ALICE. De chin.
KATHERINE. De sin. _The neck_, de nick; _the chin_, de sin.
ALICE. _Yes. Saving your honor, truly, you pronounce the words as correctly as a native of England._
KATHERINE. _I have no doubt of learning, by the grace of God, and in a short time._
ALICE. _Have you not already forgotten what I taught you?_
KATHERINE. _No, I shall recite it to you promptly:_ d'hand, de fingres, de mails,—
ALICE. De nails, _madame._
KATHERINE. De nails, de arm, de ilbow.
ALICE. _Saving your honor_, de elbow.
KATHERINE. _So I say_, d'elbow, de nick, _and_ de sin. _What do you call the foot and the gown?_
ALICE. De foot, _madame; and_ de coun.

KATHERINE. De foot _and_ de coun! _O Lord God!_—[the English words sound like crude French]—_they are words of evil sound, corrupt, vulgar, immodest, and not for ladies of honor to use. I would not pronounce these words before the lords of France for all the world. Foh!_ le foot _and_ le coun! _Nevertheless, I will recite my lesson once more in full:_ d'hand, de fingres, de nails, d'arm, d'elbow, de nick, de sin, de foot, de coun.
ALICE. _Excellent, madame!_
KATHERINE. _That is enough for one time. Let us go to dinner._
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 5 — The same
paragraphs: [Enter the King of France, the Dauphin, the Duke of Bourbon, the Constable of France and others.]
FRENCH KING. It is certain he has crossed the river Somme.
CONSTABLE. And if he is not fought with, my lord, let us not live in France—let us give up everything and hand our vineyards over to a barbarous people.

DAUPHIN. _O living God!_ Shall a few sprigs of us—the leavings of our fathers' lechery, our shoots planted in wild and savage stock—shoot up so suddenly into the clouds, and look down on the men who grafted them?
BOURBON. Normans, but bastard Normans—Norman bastards! _Death of my life_, if they march along unfought, I'll sell my dukedom to buy a slobbery and dirty farm in that jagged-cornered isle of Albion.

CONSTABLE. _God of battles_, where do they get this courage? Isn't their climate foggy, raw, and dull, where the sun looks pale on them in scorn and kills their fruit with frowns? Can boiled water—a drench for over-ridden nags, their barley-broth—boil down their cold blood to such valiant heat? And shall our quick blood, made spirited with wine, seem frosty? O, for the honor of our land, let us not hang like dripping icicles from our houses' thatch, while a frostier people sweats drops of gallant youth in our rich fields! Poor we may call them, considering their native lords.
DAUPHIN. By faith and honor, our ladies mock us, and plainly say our manhood is bred out of us, and they will give their bodies to the lust of English youth to restock France with bastard warriors.
BOURBON. They direct us to the English dancing schools to learn high lavoltas and swift corantos—saying our grace is only in our heels, and that we are most accomplished runaways.

FRENCH KING. Where is Montjoy the herald? Speed him on his way. Let him greet England with our sharp defiance. Up, princes! And, with the edge of honor sharper than your swords, hurry to the field! Charles Delabreth, High Constable of France; you Dukes of Orleans, Bourbon, and Berry, Alençon, Brabant, Bar, and Burgundy; Jacques Chatillon, Rambures, Vaudemont, Beaumont, Grandpré, Roussi, and Fauconbridge, Foix, Lestrale, Boucicault, and Charolois; high dukes, great princes, barons, lords, and knights—for the sake of your great titles, now redeem yourselves from great shames. Block this Harry of England, who sweeps through our land with banners painted in the blood of Harfleur. Rush down on his army as the melted snow does upon the valleys, whose lowly position the Alps spit and discharge their phlegm upon. Come down upon him; you have force enough. And in a captive chariot bring him our prisoner into Rouen.

CONSTABLE. This befits the great. I am sorry his numbers are so few, his soldiers sick and famished from their march; for I am sure, when he sees our army, he will drop his heart into the sink of fear and offer us his ransom as his only achievement.
FRENCH KING. Therefore, Lord Constable, hurry Montjoy on his way; and let him tell England that we send to know what willing ransom he will offer. Prince Dauphin, you shall stay with us in Rouen.
DAUPHIN. Not so, I beseech your Majesty.
FRENCH KING. Be patient—you shall remain with us. Now forth, Lord Constable and princes all, and quickly bring us word of England's fall.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 6 — The English camp in Picardy
paragraphs: [Enter Gower and Fluellen, meeting.]
GOWER. How now, Captain Fluellen! Have you come from the bridge?
FLUELLEN. I assure you, there has been very excellent service done at the bridge.
GOWER. Is the Duke of Exeter safe?

FLUELLEN. The Duke of Exeter is as great-souled as Agamemnon; a man I love and honor with my soul, my heart, my duty, my life, my livelihood, and my uttermost power. He is not—God be praised and blessed!—hurt in the world; but holds the bridge most valiantly, with excellent discipline. There is an ensign-lieutenant there at the bridge—I think in my very conscience he is as valiant a man as Mark Antony. He is a man of no reputation in the world, but I saw him do as gallant service.
GOWER. What do you call him?
FLUELLEN. He is called Ensign Pistol.
GOWER. I do not know him.
[Enter Pistol.]
FLUELLEN. Here is the man.
PISTOL. Captain, I beseech you to do me a favor. The Duke of Exeter loves you well.
FLUELLEN. Aye, I thank God; and I have earned some love at his hands.
PISTOL. Bardolph, a soldier firm and sound of heart, and of robust valor, has by cruel fate and giddy Fortune's furious fickle wheel—that blind goddess, who stands upon the rolling restless stone—

FLUELLEN. By your patience, Ensign Pistol. Fortune is painted blind, with a blindfold before her eyes, to signify to you that Fortune is blind. She is also painted with a wheel, to signify to you, which is the moral of it, that she is turning, and inconstant, and mutability, and variation; and her foot, look you, is fixed upon a spherical stone, which rolls, and rolls, and rolls. In good truth, the poet makes a most excellent description of it. Fortune is an excellent moral.

PISTOL. Fortune is Bardolph's foe, and frowns on him—for he has stolen a pax, and must be hanged. A damned death! Let gallows gape for the dog; let a man go free, and let not hemp suffocate his windpipe. But Exeter has given the doom of death for a pax of little price. Therefore, go speak; the Duke will hear your voice. And let not Bardolph's vital thread be cut by the edge of a penny cord and vile reproach. Speak, captain, for his life, and I will repay you.
FLUELLEN. Ensign Pistol, I do partly understand your meaning.
PISTOL. Why then, rejoice in it.

FLUELLEN. Certainly, ensign, it is not a thing to rejoice at. For if, look you, he were my brother, I would ask the Duke to use his good pleasure, and put him to execution. For discipline ought to be used.
PISTOL. Die and be damned! And a _fico_—a fig—for your friendship!
FLUELLEN. It is well.
PISTOL. The fig of Spain.
[Exit.]
FLUELLEN. Very good.
GOWER. Why, this is a complete counterfeit rascal. I remember him now—a pimp, a cutpurse.
FLUELLEN. I'll assure you, he uttered as brave words at the bridge as you'll see in a summer's day. But it is very well; what he has spoken to me, that is well, I warrant you, when the time comes.

GOWER. Why, he's a gull, a fool, a rogue, who now and then goes to the wars to glorify himself on his return to London under the guise of a soldier. Such fellows have the great commanders' names off by heart; and they will recite to you by rote where services were done—at such and such a redoubt, at such a breach, at such a convoy; who came off bravely, who was shot, who disgraced, what terms the enemy stood on. And this they have perfectly by heart in the language of war, which they dress up with newly-coined oaths. And what a beard cut like the general's and a horrid suit from the camp will do among foaming bottles and ale-washed wits is wonderful to consider. But you must learn to recognize such frauds of the age, or else you may be marvelously mistaken.

FLUELLEN. I tell you what, Captain Gower—I perceive he is not the man he would gladly show himself to the world to be. If I find a hole in his coat, I will tell him my mind. [Drum heard.] Hark you, the King is coming, and I must speak with him from the bridge.
[Drum and colors. Enter King Henry, Gloucester and his poor soldiers.]
God bless your Majesty!
KING HENRY V. How now, Fluellen! Have you come from the bridge?

FLUELLEN. Aye, so please your Majesty. The Duke of Exeter has very gallantly maintained the bridge. The French are gone off, look you; and there are gallant and most brave passages. By Mary, the adversary did have possession of the bridge; but he is forced to retire, and the Duke of Exeter is master of the bridge. I can tell your Majesty, the Duke is a brave man.
KING HENRY V. What men have you lost, Fluellen?

FLUELLEN. The losses of the adversary have been very great—reasonably great. By Mary, for my part, I think the Duke has lost never a man—except one who is likely to be executed for robbing a church, one Bardolph, if your Majesty knows the man. His face is all pimples, and warts, and knobs, and flames of fire; and his lips blows at his nose, and it is like a coal of fire, sometimes blue and sometimes red. But his nose is executed, and his fire's out.

KING HENRY V. We would have all such offenders so cut off. And we give express orders that in our marches through the country there be nothing taken by force from the villages, nothing taken without being paid for, none of the French abused or reviled in scornful language. For when leniency and cruelty play for a kingdom, the gentler gamester is soonest the winner.
[Tucket. Enter Montjoy.]
MONTJOY. You know me by my dress.
KING HENRY V. Well then, I know you. What shall I learn from you?
MONTJOY. My master's mind.
KING HENRY V. Unfold it.

MONTJOY. Thus says my King: Say to Harry of England—though we seemed dead, we did but sleep; advantage is a better soldier than rashness. Tell him we could have rebuked him at Harfleur, but we thought it not good to bruise an injury till it was fully ripe. Now we speak upon our cue, and our voice is imperial. England shall repent his folly, see his weakness, and admire our patience. Bid him therefore consider his ransom; which must match the losses we have borne, the subjects we have lost, the disgrace we have swallowed. Even his pettishness would bow under the weight that must answer all that. For our losses, his treasury is too poor; for the spilling of our blood, the muster of his kingdom too small a number; and for our disgrace, his own person, kneeling at our feet, only a weak and worthless satisfaction. To this add defiance; and tell him, in conclusion, he has betrayed his followers, whose condemnation has been pronounced. So far my King and master; so much my office.
KING HENRY V. What is your name? I know your office.
MONTJOY. Montjoy.

KING HENRY V. You do your office fairly. Turn yourself back, and tell your King I do not seek him now, but could be willing to march on to Calais without challenge. For, to tell the truth—though it's no wisdom to admit so much to a wily and well-positioned enemy—my people are much weakened by sickness, my numbers lessened, and those few I have are almost no better than so many Frenchmen. When they were in health, I tell you, herald, I reckoned one pair of English legs could march down three Frenchmen. Yet, forgive me, God, that I brag thus! This air of France of yours has blown that vice into me. I must repent. Go therefore, and tell your master: here I am. My ransom is this frail and worthless body; my army only a weak and sickly guard. Yet, with God before us, tell him we will come on, though France himself and such another neighbor stand in our way. There—for your labor, Montjoy. Go, bid your master well advise himself. If we may pass, we will; if we are hindered, we shall discolor your tawny ground with your red blood. And so, Montjoy, fare you well. The sum of all our answer is just this: we would not seek a battle, as we are; nor, as we are, do we say we will shun it. So tell your master.
MONTJOY. I shall deliver it so. Thanks to your Highness.
[Exit.]
GLOUCESTER. I hope they will not come upon us now.
KING HENRY V. We are in God's hands, brother, not in theirs. March to the bridge; it now draws toward night. Beyond the river we'll encamp ourselves, and tomorrow bid them march away.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 7 — The French camp, near Agincourt
paragraphs: [Enter the Constable of France, the Lord Rambures, Orleans, Dauphin with others.]
CONSTABLE. Tut! I have the best armor in the world. I wish it were day!
ORLEANS. You have excellent armor; but let my horse have his due.
CONSTABLE. It is the best horse in Europe.
ORLEANS. Will it never be morning?
DAUPHIN. My Lord of Orleans, and my Lord High Constable—you talk of horse and armor?
ORLEANS. You are as well provided with both as any prince in the world.

DAUPHIN. What a long night this is! I wouldn't trade my horse with any creature that walks on four hooves. Ha! He bounds off the earth as if his guts were springs—_le cheval volant_, the flying horse, the Pegasus, _qui a les narines de feu!_—with nostrils of fire! When I mount him, I soar—I am a hawk. He trots the air; the earth sings when he touches it; the lowest horn of his hoof is more musical than the pipe of Hermes.
ORLEANS. He's the color of nutmeg.

DAUPHIN. And as hot as ginger. He's a beast for Perseus. He is pure air and fire; and the dull elements of earth and water never appear in him, except in patient stillness while his rider mounts him. He is indeed a horse; all the other nags you may call beasts.
CONSTABLE. Indeed, my lord, he is a most absolute and excellent horse.
DAUPHIN. He is the prince of palfreys; his neigh is like the command of a monarch, and his very countenance demands homage.
ORLEANS. No more, cousin.

DAUPHIN. No, the man has no wit who cannot, from the lark's rising to the lamb's bedding, vary his deserved praise of my palfrey. It's a subject as fluent as the sea; turn the sands into eloquent tongues, and my horse is theme enough for them all. It's a subject for a sovereign to reason on, and for a sovereign's sovereign to ride on; and for the whole world—familiar and unknown—to lay aside their particular concerns and wonder at him. I once wrote a sonnet in his praise and it began thus: "Wonder of nature"—
ORLEANS. I have heard a sonnet to one's mistress begin so.
DAUPHIN. Then they imitated what I composed for my courser—for my horse is my mistress.
ORLEANS. Your mistress bears well.
DAUPHIN. Bears me well—which is the prescribed praise and perfection of a good and particular mistress.
CONSTABLE. Indeed, for I thought yesterday your mistress shrewdly shook your back.
DAUPHIN. So perhaps did yours.
CONSTABLE. Mine was not bridled.
DAUPHIN. O, then no doubt she was old and gentle; and you rode like a foot-soldier of Ireland, with your French breeches off, in your tight stockings.
CONSTABLE. You have good judgment in horsemanship.
DAUPHIN. Be warned by me, then. Those who ride that way, and not carefully, fall into foul bogs. I'd rather have my horse for my mistress.
CONSTABLE. I'd as soon have my mistress a jade.
DAUPHIN. I tell you, Constable, my mistress wears his own hair.
CONSTABLE. I could make as true a boast as that, if my mistress were a sow.
DAUPHIN. "_Le chien est retourné à son propre vomissement, et la truie lavée au bourbier_"—The dog is returned to his own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mire. You'll use anything.
CONSTABLE. Yet I don't use my horse for my mistress, or any such proverb so little related to the point.
RAMBURES. My Lord Constable, the armor I saw in your tent tonight—are those stars or suns upon it?
CONSTABLE. Stars, my lord.
DAUPHIN. Some of them will fall tomorrow, I hope.
CONSTABLE. And yet my sky shall not lack any.
DAUPHIN. That may be, for you wear many extras—and it would be more honor if some were gone.
CONSTABLE. Even as your horse bears your praises—who would trot as well, if some of your brags were dismounted.
DAUPHIN. I wish I could load him with the praises he deserves! Will it never be day? Tomorrow I will trot a mile, and my path shall be paved with English faces.
CONSTABLE. I will not say so, for fear I should be faced out of my path. But I wish it were morning—for I'd gladly be at the ears of the English.
RAMBURES. Who will gamble with me for twenty prisoners?
CONSTABLE. You must first risk yourself, before you have them.
DAUPHIN. It is midnight; I'll go arm myself.
[Exit.]
ORLEANS. The Dauphin longs for morning.
RAMBURES. He longs to eat the English.
CONSTABLE. I think he will eat all he kills.
ORLEANS. By the white hand of my lady, he's a gallant prince.
CONSTABLE. Swear by her foot, that she may tread out the oath.
ORLEANS. He is simply the most active gentleman of France.
CONSTABLE. Doing is activity; and he will still be doing.
ORLEANS. He never did harm, that I heard of.
CONSTABLE. Nor will he do any tomorrow. He'll keep up that good reputation.
ORLEANS. I know him to be valiant.
CONSTABLE. I was told that by one who knows him better than you.
ORLEANS. Who's that?
CONSTABLE. By Mary, he told me so himself—and he said he didn't care who knew it.
ORLEANS. He doesn't need to care; it's no hidden virtue in him.
CONSTABLE. By my faith, sir, it is. Nobody ever saw it but his lackey. It's a hooded valor—and when it does appear, it will diminish.
ORLEANS. "Ill will never said well."
CONSTABLE. I'll match that proverb with "There is flattery in friendship."
ORLEANS. And I'll top that with "Give the devil his due."
CONSTABLE. Well placed. There stands your friend for the devil; have at the very eye of that proverb with "A pox of the devil."
ORLEANS. You are the better at proverbs, by how much "A fool's bolt is soon shot."
CONSTABLE. You've shot too far.
ORLEANS. It's not the first time you were overshot.
[Enter a Messenger.]
MESSENGER. My Lord High Constable, the English are within fifteen hundred paces of your tents.
CONSTABLE. Who measured the ground?
MESSENGER. The Lord Grandpré.
CONSTABLE. A valiant and most expert gentleman. I wish it were day! Alas, poor Harry of England—he doesn't long for the dawn as we do.
ORLEANS. What a wretched and peevish fellow this King of England is—to mope with his fat-brained followers so far out of his element!
CONSTABLE. If the English had any understanding, they would run away.
ORLEANS. That's what they lack; for if their heads had any intellectual armor, they could never wear such heavy helmets.
RAMBURES. That island of England breeds very valiant creatures. Their mastiffs are of unmatchable courage.

ORLEANS. Foolish curs, that run blindly into the mouth of a Russian bear and have their heads crushed like rotten apples! You may as well say that flea is valiant which dares to eat his breakfast on the lip of a lion.

CONSTABLE. Just so, just so; and the men match their mastiffs in robust and rough charging, leaving their wits with their wives. Then, give them great meals of beef and iron and steel, and they will eat like wolves and fight like devils.
ORLEANS. Aye, but these English are notably short of beef.
CONSTABLE. Then we shall find tomorrow that they have only stomachs to eat, and none to fight. Now is the time to arm. Come, shall we be about it?
ORLEANS. It is now two o'clock; but, let me see, by ten we shall each have a hundred Englishmen.
[Exeunt.]
[Enter Chorus.]

CHORUS. Now entertain the thought of a time when creeping murmur and the searching darkness fills the wide vessel of the universe. From camp to camp through the foul womb of night the hum of each army quietly sounds, so that the fixed sentinels almost catch the secret whispers of each other's watch. Fire answers fire; and through their pale flames each army sees the other's shadowed face. Horse threatens horse, in high and boastful neighs piercing the night's dull ear. And from the tents the armorers, fitting out the knights, with busy hammers closing rivets up, give dreadful sound of preparation. The country cocks crow, the clocks chime, and name the third hour of drowsy morning. Proud of their numbers and secure in soul, the confident and over-eager French play dice for the lowly-rated English; and chide the limping cripple Night, who like a foul and ugly witch limps so tediously away. The poor condemned English, like sacrifices, sit patiently by their watchful fires and inwardly ruminate on the morning's danger; and their sad bearing, set on lank-lean cheeks and war-worn coats, presents them to the gazing moon as so many horrid ghosts. O, now—who will behold the royal captain of this ruined band walking from watch to watch, from tent to tent—let him cry, "Praise and glory on his head!" For forth he goes and visits all his host, bids them good morning with a modest smile, and calls them brothers, friends, and countrymen. Upon his royal face there is no sign of how dreadful an army has surrounded him; nor does he give one jot of color to the weary and all-watched night, but looks fresh, and overcomes weariness with cheerful appearance and sweet majesty. Every wretch, pining and pale before, on seeing him plucks comfort from his looks. A universal bounty like the sun his liberal eye gives to everyone, thawing cold fear, so that all—low and gentle—behold, as unworthiness may define, a little touch of Harry in the night. And so our scene must fly to the battle—where, O for pity, we shall much disgrace, with four or five most vile and ragged foils ill-arranged in a ridiculous brawl, the name of Agincourt. Yet sit and watch, picturing the true things by their mock representations.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — The English camp at Agincourt
