paragraphs: [Enter King Henry, Bedford and Gloucester.]

KING HENRY V. Gloucester, it is true that we are in great danger; the greater therefore must our courage be. Good morning, brother Bedford. God Almighty! There is some soul of goodness in evil things, if men would observingly distill it out. Our bad neighbor makes us early risers, which is both healthful and good husbandry. Besides, they are our outward consciences, and preachers to us all, warning us to prepare ourselves fairly for our end. Thus we may gather honey from the weed, and make a moral lesson of the devil himself.
[Enter Erpingham.]
Good morning, old Sir Thomas Erpingham. A good soft pillow for that good white head would be better than a churlish turf of France.
ERPINGHAM. Not so, my liege; this lodging pleases me better, since I can say, "Now I lie like a king."

KING HENRY V. It is good for men to love their present hardships by example; so the spirit is eased. And when the mind is quickened, no doubt, the limbs, though dead and inert before, break out of their drowsy grave and move freshly, with cast-off skin and new agility. Lend me your cloak, Sir Thomas. Brothers both, commend me to the princes in our camp; give them my good morning, and presently bid them all to my pavilion.
GLOUCESTER. We shall, my liege.
ERPINGHAM. Shall I attend your Grace?
KING HENRY V. No, my good knight. Go with my brothers to my lords of England. I and my heart must debate awhile, and then I want no other company.
ERPINGHAM. The Lord in heaven bless you, noble Harry!
[Exeunt all but King.]
KING HENRY V. God thank you, old heart! You speak cheerfully.
[Enter Pistol.]
PISTOL. _Qui vous là?_—Who goes there?
KING HENRY V. A friend.
PISTOL. Explain to me—are you an officer? Or are you a base, common, ordinary fellow?
KING HENRY V. I am a gentleman of a company.
PISTOL. Do you carry the mighty pike?
KING HENRY V. Even so. What are you?
PISTOL. As good a gentleman as the Emperor.
KING HENRY V. Then you are better than the King.

PISTOL. The King's a fine fellow, and a heart of gold; a lad of life, an imp of fame; of good parents, of fist most valiant. I kiss his dirty shoe, and from my heartstrings I love the lovely brave one. What is your name?
KING HENRY V. Harry le Roy.
PISTOL. Le Roy! A Cornish name. Are you of a Cornish crew?
KING HENRY V. No, I am a Welshman.
PISTOL. Do you know Fluellen?
KING HENRY V. Yes.
PISTOL. Tell him I'll knock his leek about his head on Saint David's Day.
KING HENRY V. Don't you wear your dagger in your cap that day, in case he should knock that about yours.
PISTOL. Are you his friend?
KING HENRY V. And his kinsman too.
PISTOL. A _fico_—a fig—for you, then!
KING HENRY V. I thank you. God be with you!
PISTOL. My name is Pistol, so they call me.
[Exit.]
KING HENRY V. It suits well with your fierceness.
[Enter Fluellen and Gower.]
GOWER. Captain Fluellen!

FLUELLEN. So! In the name of Jesus Christ, speak lower. It is the greatest wonder in all the universal world when the true and ancient prerogatives and laws of war are not kept. If you would take the trouble just to examine the wars of Pompey the Great, you shall find, I warrant you, that there is no tittle-tattle or pibble-pabble in Pompey's camp. I warrant you, you shall find the ceremonies of war, and the care of it, and the forms of it, and the sobriety of it, and the modesty of it, to be otherwise.
GOWER. Why, the enemy is loud; you hear him all night.

FLUELLEN. If the enemy is an ass and a fool and a prating coxcomb, is it fitting, do you think, that we should also, look you, be an ass and a fool and a prating coxcomb? Speak to your own conscience, now.
GOWER. I will speak lower.
FLUELLEN. I pray you and beseech you that you will.
[Exeunt Gower and Fluellen.]
KING HENRY V. Though it appears a little out of fashion, there is much care and valor in this Welshman.
[Enter three soldiers, John Bates, Alexander Court and Michael Williams.]
COURT. Brother John Bates, is that not the morning breaking yonder?
BATES. I think it is. But we have no great cause to desire the approach of day.
WILLIAMS. We see yonder the beginning of the day, but I think we shall never see the end of it. Who goes there?
KING HENRY V. A friend.
WILLIAMS. Under what captain do you serve?
KING HENRY V. Under Sir Thomas Erpingham.
WILLIAMS. A good old commander and a most kind gentleman. Pray, what does he think of our condition?
KING HENRY V. Even as men wrecked upon a sandbar, who expect to be washed off by the next tide.
BATES. Has he told his thought to the King?

KING HENRY V. No; nor is it fitting that he should. For though I say it to you, I think the King is just a man as I am. The violet smells to him as it does to me; the elements appear to him as they do to me; all his senses have only human conditions. With his ceremonies laid aside, in his nakedness he appears only a man. And though his feelings are mounted higher than ours, yet when they come down, they come down with the same wing. Therefore, when he sees reason for fear as we do, his fears, without doubt, are of the same flavor as ours. Yet, in reason, no man should fill him with any show of fear, lest he, by showing it, should dishearten his army.

BATES. He may show what outward courage he will; but I believe, cold a night as it is, he could wish himself in the Thames up to the neck. And so I'd have him be, and I beside him, come what may, so we were quit of this place.
KING HENRY V. By my troth, I'll speak my conscience about the King: I think he would not wish himself anywhere but where he is.
BATES. Then I wish he were here alone; that way he'd be sure to be ransomed, and many poor men's lives would be saved.

KING HENRY V. I dare say you love him not so badly as to wish him here alone, however you say this to feel out other men's minds. I think I could not die anywhere as contented as in the King's company, his cause being just and his quarrel honorable.
WILLIAMS. That's more than we know.
BATES. Aye, or more than we should look into. For we know enough, if we know we are the King's subjects. If his cause is wrong, our obedience to the King wipes the crime of it out of us.

WILLIAMS. But if the cause is not good, the King himself has a heavy reckoning to make—when all those legs and arms and heads, chopped off in battle, shall join together at the Last Day and cry all together, "We died at such a place"; some swearing, some crying for a surgeon, some about the wives they left poor behind them, some about the debts they owe, some about the children left rawly behind. I'm afraid there are few who die well that die in battle—for how can they charitably dispose of anything, when blood is their argument? Now, if these men do not die well, it will be a black matter for the King who led them to it—whom to disobey would be against all proper subjection.

KING HENRY V. So, if a son sent by his father on a trading errand sinfully perishes at sea, by your rule the blame for his wickedness should be put upon the father who sent him. Or if a servant, under his master's command transporting a sum of money, is set upon by robbers and dies in many unconfessed sins, you may say the master's business is the cause of the servant's damnation. But this is not so. The King is not bound to answer for the particular ends of his soldiers, the father for his son, nor the master for his servant; for they do not plan their death when they plan their service. Besides, there is no king, no matter how spotless his cause, who can, if it comes to the arbitration of swords, try it out with all unspotted soldiers. Some perhaps have on them the guilt of premeditated and contrived murder; some, of beguiling virgins with the broken seals of perjury; some, making the wars their refuge, who have before gored the gentle bosom of Peace with pillage and robbery. Now, if these men have escaped the law and outrun native punishment, though they can outrun men, they have no wings to fly from God. War is His sergeant, war is His vengeance—so that here men are punished for their previous breaches of the King's laws, now in the King's quarrel. Where they feared death, they have brought life away; and where they would be safe, they perish. Then if they die unprepared, the King is no more guilty of their damnation than he was before guilty of those impieties for which they are now visited. Every subject's duty is the King's; but every subject's soul is his own. Therefore every soldier in the wars should do as every sick man in his bed: wash every mote out of his conscience. Dying so, death is to his advantage; or, not dying, the time was blessedly spent in which such preparation was gained. And in him who escapes, it would not be a sin to think that, his having made God so free an offer, He let him outlive that day to see His greatness, and to teach others how they should prepare.
WILLIAMS. It is certain—every man who dies ill, the ill is upon his own head; the King is not to answer for it.
BATES. I don't ask him to answer for me; and yet I'm determined to fight lustily for him.
KING HENRY V. I myself heard the King say he would not be ransomed.
WILLIAMS. Aye, he said so to make us fight cheerfully. But when our throats are cut, he may be ransomed, and we'll be none the wiser.
KING HENRY V. If I live to see it, I will never trust his word after.

WILLIAMS. You'll pay him out, then! That's a fearful shot out of a popgun—what a poor private grievance can do against a monarch! You might as well try to turn the sun to ice by fanning his face with a peacock's feather. "You'll never trust his word after!" Come, it's a foolish saying.
KING HENRY V. Your rebuke is a touch too blunt. I'd be angry with you, if the time were right.
WILLIAMS. Let it be a quarrel between us, if you live.
KING HENRY V. I accept it.
WILLIAMS. How shall I know you again?
KING HENRY V. Give me any token of yours, and I'll wear it in my hat; then, if you ever dare acknowledge it, I'll make it my quarrel.
WILLIAMS. Here's my glove; give me another of yours.
KING HENRY V. There.
WILLIAMS. This I will also wear in my cap. If ever you come to me, after tomorrow, and say, "This is my glove," by this hand I will take you a box on the ear.
KING HENRY V. If ever I live to see it, I will claim it.
WILLIAMS. You'd as soon be hanged.
KING HENRY V. Well, I will do it, even if I take you in the King's company.
WILLIAMS. Keep your word; fare you well.
BATES. Be friends, you English fools, be friends. We have French quarrels enough, if you could think how to count them.

KING HENRY V. Indeed, the French may bet twenty French crowns to one that they will beat us, for they bear them on their shoulders. But it's no English treason to cut—or clip—French crowns; and tomorrow the King himself will be a clipper.
[Exeunt soldiers.]

Upon the King! Let our lives, our souls, our debts, our anxious wives, our children, and our sins lay on the King! We must bear it all. O hard condition, twin-born with greatness, subject to the breath of every fool—whose understanding can feel nothing but his own wringing! What infinite heart's ease must kings give up that private men enjoy! And what do kings have that ordinary men don't have too, except ceremony—just general ceremony? And what are you, you idol Ceremony? What kind of god are you, that suffer more of mortal griefs than your worshippers do? What are your rents? What are your incomes? O Ceremony, show me only your worth! What is your soul of adoration? Are you anything more than place, degree, and form, creating awe and fear in other men? In which you are less happy being feared than they are in fearing. What do you drink, often, instead of sweet homage, but poisoned flattery? O, be sick, great greatness, and bid your Ceremony give you cure! Do you think the fiery fever will go out by titles blown from flattery? Will it give way to bowing and low scraping? Can you, when you command the beggar's knee, command its health? No, you proud dream, who play so subtly with a king's repose. I am a king who finds you out, and I know it is not the balm, the scepter, and the orb, the sword, the mace, the imperial crown, the inwoven robe of gold and pearl, the swollen title running before the King, the throne he sits on, nor the tide of pomp that beats upon the high shore of this world—no, not all these, thrice-gorgeous Ceremony, not all these, laid in royal bed, can sleep as soundly as the wretched slave who, with a body full and an empty mind, gets him to rest, crammed with bread of distress, never sees horrid night, the child of hell, but, like a lackey, from sunrise to sunset sweats in the eye of Phoebus, and all night sleeps in Elysium. Next day after dawn he rises, and helps Hyperion mount his horse, and so follows the ever-running year, with profitable labor, to his grave. And, but for ceremony, such a wretch—winding up days with toil and nights with sleep—would have the lead and advantage over a king. The slave, a member of the country's peace, enjoys it; but in his thick brain he little knows what watch the King keeps to maintain the peace whose hours the peasant most enjoys.
[Enter Erpingham.]
ERPINGHAM. My lord, your nobles, anxious at your absence, seek through your camp to find you.
KING HENRY V. Good old knight, gather them all together at my tent. I'll be there before you.
ERPINGHAM. I shall do it, my lord.
[Exit.]

KING HENRY V. O God of battles! Steel my soldiers' hearts. Do not fill them with fear. Take from them now the sense of counting numbers, if the opposing forces would pluck their hearts from them. Not today, O Lord, O, not today—do not think upon the fault my father made in seizing the crown! I have buried Richard's body anew, and have bestowed upon it more contrite tears than ever forced drops of blood issued from it. Five hundred poor I have on yearly wages, who twice a day hold their withered hands up toward heaven to pardon the blood. And I have built two chantries, where sad and solemn priests still sing for Richard's soul. More will I do—though all that I can do is worth nothing, since my penance comes after all, imploring pardon.
[Enter Gloucester.]
GLOUCESTER. My liege!
KING HENRY V. My brother Gloucester's voice? Yes. I know your errand—I'll go with you. The day, my friends, and all things stay for me.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — The French camp
paragraphs: [Enter the Dauphin, Orleans, Rambures and others.]
ORLEANS. The sun gilds our armor; up, my lords!
DAUPHIN. _Monte à cheval!_—To horse! My horse, _varlet! laquais_—lackey! ha!
ORLEANS. O brave spirit!
DAUPHIN. _Via, les eaux et terre!_—Away, water and earth!
ORLEANS. _Rien puis? L'air et feu?_—Nothing more? Air and fire?
DAUPHIN. _Cieux_—heavens, cousin Orleans.
[Enter Constable.]
Now, my Lord Constable!
CONSTABLE. Hark, how our steeds neigh ready for the action!
DAUPHIN. Mount them and make incisions in their hides, so that their hot blood may spin in English eyes, and douse those eyes with our overflowing courage, ha!
RAMBURES. What, will you make them weep our horses' blood? How shall we then see their natural tears?
[Enter a Messenger.]
MESSENGER. The English are drawn up in battle order, you French peers.

CONSTABLE. To horse, you gallant princes! Straight to horse! Just look at that poor and starved band, and your fair show shall suck away their souls, leaving them only the shells and husks of men. There is not work enough for all our hands; barely blood enough in all their sickly veins to give each naked cutlass a stain that our French gallants shall today draw out, and sheathe again for lack of sport. Let us just breathe on them—the vapor of our valor will overturn them. It is certain, beyond all exceptions, lords, that our extra lackeys and our peasants, who swarm in unnecessary action about our squares of battle, would be enough to purge this field of such a worthless foe—though we upon this mountain's base stood by for idle observation, but that our honor will not permit it. What's to say? Just a very little, let us do, and all is done. Then let the trumpets sound the fanfare and the note to mount. For our approach shall so much daunt the field that England shall crouch down in fear and yield.
[Enter Grandpré.]

GRANDPRÉ. Why do you delay so long, my lords of France? Yonder island carcasses, despairing of their bones, ill-favoredly disgrace the morning field. Their tattered banners are loosely flying, and our air shakes them passing scornfully. Mighty Mars looks bankrupt in their beggared host, and faintly peeks through a rusty visor. The horsemen sit like fixed candlesticks with torch-staves in their hand; and their poor nags hang down their heads, drooping their hides and hips, the gum dripping down from their pale dead eyes, and in their pale dull mouths the jointed bit lies foul with chewed grass, still and motionless. And their undertakers, the knavish crows, fly over them, impatient for their hour. Description cannot find words enough to demonstrate the life of such a battle—so lifeless does it appear.
CONSTABLE. They have said their prayers, and they wait for death.
DAUPHIN. Shall we go send them dinners, and fresh clothes, and give their starving horses fodder, and then fight with them?
CONSTABLE. I wait only for my guard; on to the field! I'll take the banner from a trumpeter, and use it in my haste. Come, come, away! The sun is high, and we are wasting the day.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — The English camp
paragraphs: [Enter Gloucester, Bedford, Exeter, Erpingham, with all his host: Salisbury and Westmorland.]
GLOUCESTER. Where is the King?
BEDFORD. The King himself has ridden out to view their battle line.
WESTMORLAND. Of fighting men they have a full sixty thousand.
EXETER. That's five to one—besides, they are all fresh.

SALISBURY. God's arm strike with us! It's a fearful odds. God be with you, princes all; I go to my command. If we meet no more until we meet in heaven, then, joyfully, my noble Lord of Bedford, my dear Lord Gloucester, and my good Lord Exeter, and my kind kinsman, warriors all—adieu!
BEDFORD. Farewell, good Salisbury, and good luck go with you!
EXETER. Farewell, kind lord; fight valiantly today! And yet I do you wrong to remind you of it—for you are framed out of the firm truth of valor.
[Exit Salisbury.]
BEDFORD. He is as full of valor as of kindness—princely in both.
[Enter the King.]
WESTMORLAND. O, that we now had here just one ten thousand of those men in England who are doing no work today!

KING HENRY V. What man wishes so? My cousin Westmorland? No, my fair cousin. If we are marked to die, we are enough to do our country loss; and if to live, the fewer men, the greater the share of honor. God's will! I pray you, wish not one man more. By Jove, I am not greedy for gold, nor do I care who is fed at my expense. It does not gnaw at me if men wear my garments. Such outward things do not live in my desires. But if it is a sin to covet honor, I am the most offending soul alive. No, faith, my cousin, wish not one man from England. God's peace! I would not lose so great an honor as one more man, I think, would share from me, for the best hope I have. O, do not wish one more! Rather proclaim it, Westmorland, through my host, that whoever has no stomach for this fight, let him depart. His passport shall be made, and crowns for travel put into his purse. We would not die in that man's company who fears his fellowship to die with us. This day is called the feast of Crispian. He that outlives this day, and comes safe home, will stand on tiptoe whenever this day is named, and rouse himself at the name of Crispian. He that shall live to see old age will yearly on the vigil feast his neighbors, and say, "Tomorrow is Saint Crispian." Then will he strip his sleeve and show his scars, and say, "These wounds I had on Crispian's day." Old men forget; yet all shall be forgotten, but he'll remember, with embellishments, what deeds he did that day. Then shall our names, familiar in his mouth as household words—Harry the King, Bedford and Exeter, Warwick and Talbot, Salisbury and Gloucester—be freshly remembered as their cups overflow. This story shall the good man teach his son; and Crispin Crispian shall never go by, from this day to the ending of the world, but we in it shall be remembered—we few, we happy few, we band of brothers. For he today that sheds his blood with me shall be my brother; be he ever so lowly, this day shall gentle his condition. And gentlemen in England now abed shall think themselves accursed they were not here, and hold their manhood cheap while any man speaks who fought with us upon Saint Crispin's day.
[Enter Salisbury.]
SALISBURY. My sovereign lord, place yourself at speed. The French are bravely set in their battle order, and will charge upon us with all dispatch.
KING HENRY V. All things are ready, if our minds are so.
WESTMORLAND. Perish the man whose mind is hanging back now!
KING HENRY V. You don't wish more help from England now, cousin?
WESTMORLAND. God's will! My liege, I wish you and I alone, without more help, could fight this royal battle!
KING HENRY V. Why, now you have unwished five thousand men—which pleases me better than to wish even one more for us. You know your places. God be with you all!
[Tucket. Enter Montjoy.]

MONTJOY. Once more I come to know of you, King Harry, if you will now agree to your ransom before your most assured overthrow. For certainly you are so near the abyss that you must be swallowed up. Besides, in mercy, the Constable wishes you to remind your followers of repentance—so that their souls may make a peaceful and a sweet retreat from off these fields where, wretches, their poor bodies must lie and fester.
KING HENRY V. Who has sent you now?
MONTJOY. The Constable of France.

KING HENRY V. I pray you, take my former answer back: tell them to defeat me first, then sell my bones. Good God! Why should they mock poor fellows so? The man who once sold the lion's skin while the beast was still alive was killed in hunting it. Many of our bodies shall no doubt find native graves, upon which, I trust, witness shall live in brass of this day's work; and those who leave their valiant bones in France, dying like men, though buried in your dunghills—they shall be famous. For there the sun shall greet them, and draw their honors steaming up to heaven, leaving their earthly parts to choke your air—the smell of which shall breed a plague in France. Then mark the abounding valor in our English, who being dead, like a bullet's ricochet, break out into a second round of mischief, killing even in death's relapse. Let me speak proudly: tell the Constable—we are only warriors for the working day. Our finery and our gilt are all besmirched with rainy marching in the painful field. There's not a feather left in all our army—good evidence, I hope, that we will not fly—and time has worn us into shabbiness. But, by the mass, our hearts are trim. And my poor soldiers tell me that, before night, they'll be in fresher robes, or they'll pluck the gay new coats off the French soldiers' heads and turn them out of service. If they do this—as, please God, they shall—my ransom then will soon be raised. Herald, save your labor. Come no more for ransom, gentle herald. They shall have none, I swear, but these my joints; which if they have, as I will leave them to them, shall yield them little—tell the Constable.
MONTJOY. I shall, King Harry. And so fare you well; you shall never hear a herald any more.
[Exit.]
KING HENRY V. I fear you'll come once more again for ransom.
[Enter York.]
YORK. My lord, most humbly on my knee I beg the leadership of the vanguard.
KING HENRY V. Take it, brave York. Now, soldiers, march away; and dispose the day, God, however you please!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — The field of battle
paragraphs: [Alarum. Excursions. Enter Pistol, French Soldier and Boy.]
PISTOL. Yield, you cur!
FRENCH SOLDIER. _Je pense que vous êtes le gentilhomme de bonne qualité._—I think you are a gentleman of good quality.
PISTOL. _Qualité? Caleno custore me!_ Are you a gentleman? What is your name? Speak up.
FRENCH SOLDIER. _O Seigneur Dieu!_—O Lord God!

PISTOL. O, Signieur Dew must be a gentleman. Mark my words, O Signieur Dew, and pay attention: O Signieur Dew, you die on the point of my sword, unless, O signieur, you give to me an outrageous ransom.
FRENCH SOLDIER. _O, prenez miséricorde! Ayez pitié de moi!_—O, have mercy! Take pity on me!
PISTOL. "Moy" shall not serve; I will have forty moys—or I will fetch your guts out at your throat in drops of crimson blood.
FRENCH SOLDIER. _Est-il impossible d'échapper la force de ton bras?_—Is it impossible to escape the force of your arm?
PISTOL. Brass, you cur! You damned and lewd mountain goat, you offer me brass?
FRENCH SOLDIER. _O pardonnez-moi!_—O forgive me!
PISTOL. Do you say that to me? Is that a ton of moys? Come here, boy; ask this slave in French what his name is.
BOY. _Écoutez. Comment êtes-vous appelé?_—Listen. What are you called?
FRENCH SOLDIER. _Monsieur le Fer._
BOY. He says his name is Master Fer.
PISTOL. Master Fer! I'll fer him, and firk him, and ferret him. Tell him the same in French.
BOY. I do not know the French for "fer," and "ferret," and "firk."
PISTOL. Tell him to get ready; for I will cut his throat.
FRENCH SOLDIER. _Que dit-il, monsieur?_—What does he say, sir?

BOY. _Il me commande à vous dire que vous faites vous prêt, car ce soldat ici est disposé tout à cette heure de couper votre gorge._—He commands me to tell you to make yourself ready, for this soldier here is disposed at this very hour to cut your throat.
PISTOL. Aye, _couper la gorge_—cut the throat—_par ma foi_, by my faith, peasant, unless you give me crowns, brave crowns; or mangled you shall be by this my sword.

FRENCH SOLDIER. _O, je vous supplie, pour l'amour de Dieu, me pardonner! Je suis le gentilhomme de bonne maison; gardez ma vie, et je vous donnerai deux cents écus._—O, I beg you, for the love of God, pardon me! I am a gentleman of good house; spare my life, and I will give you two hundred crowns.
PISTOL. What are his words?
BOY. He prays you to save his life. He is a gentleman of a good house; and for his ransom he will give you two hundred crowns.
PISTOL. Tell him my fury shall abate, and I will take the crowns.
FRENCH SOLDIER. _Petit monsieur, que dit-il?_—Little sir, what does he say?

BOY. _Encore qu'il est contre son jurement de pardonner aucun prisonnier; néanmoins, pour les écus que vous lui avez promis, il est content à vous donner la liberté, le franchisement._—Though it is against his oath to pardon any prisoner; nevertheless, for the crowns you have promised him, he is content to give you your liberty, your freedom.

FRENCH SOLDIER. _Sur mes genoux je vous donne mille remerciements; et je m'estime heureux que je suis tombé entre les mains d'un chevalier, je pense, le plus brave, vaillant, et très distingué seigneur d'Angleterre._—On my knees I give you a thousand thanks; and I count myself happy that I have fallen into the hands of one knight, I think, the most brave, valiant, and very distinguished lord of England.
PISTOL. Explain to me, boy.

BOY. He gives you, upon his knees, a thousand thanks; and he counts himself happy that he has fallen into the hands of one whom he thinks the most brave, valorous, and thrice-worthy _seigneur_ of England.
PISTOL. As I suck blood, I will show some mercy. Follow me!
BOY. _Suivez-vous le grand capitaine._—Follow the great captain.
[Exeunt Pistol and French Soldier.]

I have never known so full a voice come out of so empty a heart; but the saying is true: "The empty vessel makes the greatest sound." Bardolph and Nym had ten times more valor than this roaring devil from the old play, whose nails anyone may pare with a wooden dagger. And they are both hanged; and so would this one be, if he dared steal anything daringly. I must stay with the lackeys at the baggage of our camp. The French might have a fine prize from us, if he knew of it; for there is none to guard it but boys.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 5 — Another part of the field
paragraphs: [Enter Constable, Orleans, Bourbon, Dauphin and Rambures.]
CONSTABLE. _O diable!_—O devil!
ORLEANS. _O Seigneur! le jour est perdu, tout est perdu!_—O Lord! The day is lost, all is lost!
DAUPHIN. _Mort de ma vie!_—Death of my life! All is ruined, all! Reproach and everlasting shame sit mocking in our plumes.
[A short alarum.]
_O méchante Fortune!_—O wicked Fortune!—Do not run away.
CONSTABLE. Why, all our ranks are broken.
DAUPHIN. O lasting shame! Let's stab ourselves. Are these the wretches we played at dice for?
ORLEANS. Is this the king we sent to for his ransom?

BOURBON. Shame and eternal shame—nothing but shame! Let's die in honor! Once more back into it! And whoever will not follow Bourbon now, let him go away, and with cap in hand, like a base pimp, hold the chamber door while by a slave, no nobler than my dog, his fairest daughter is contaminated.
CONSTABLE. Disorder, that has spoiled us, befriend us now! Let us go in heaps and offer up our lives.
ORLEANS. We are enough still living in the field to smother the English in our throngs, if any order could be thought of.
BOURBON. The devil take order now! I'll to the throng. Let life be short, else shame will be too long.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 6 — Another part of the field
paragraphs: [Alarum. Enter King Henry and his train, with prisoners.]
KING HENRY V. Well have we done, thrice valiant countrymen. But all is not done; yet the French still hold the field.
EXETER. The Duke of York commends himself to your Majesty.
KING HENRY V. Does he live, good uncle? Three times within this hour I saw him down; three times up again, and fighting. From helmet to spur he was all blood.

EXETER. In that condition, brave soldier, he lies, larding the plain; and by his bloody side, yoked together with his honor-earning wounds, the noble Earl of Suffolk also lies. Suffolk died first; and York, all hacked over, comes to him where he lay steeped in gore, and takes him by the beard; kisses the gashes that bloodily gaped upon his face. He cries aloud, "Tarry, my cousin Suffolk! My soul shall keep yours company to heaven; tarry, sweet soul, for mine, then fly abreast, as in this glorious and well-fought field we kept together in our chivalry." Upon these words I came up and cheered him on. He smiled at me, reached me his hand, and with a feeble grip says, "Dear my lord, commend my service to my sovereign." Then he turned and over Suffolk's neck he threw his wounded arm and kissed his lips; and so wedded to death, he sealed with blood a testament of noble-ending love. The sweet and tender manner of it forced from me those tears which I would have stopped; but I hadn't so much of man in me—all my mother came into my eyes and gave me up to tears.
KING HENRY V. I do not blame you. For hearing this, I must of necessity compound with misty eyes, or they too will overflow.
[Alarum.]
But hark! What new alarm is this? The French have reinforced their scattered men. Then let every soldier kill his prisoners; pass the order along.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 7 — Another part of the field
paragraphs: [Enter Fluellen and Gower.]
FLUELLEN. Kill the boys and the baggage! It is expressly against the law of arms. It is as outright a piece of knavery, mark you now, as can be offered. In your own conscience, now, is it not?

GOWER. It is certain there's not a boy left alive; and the cowardly rascals who ran from the battle have done this slaughter. Besides, they have burned and carried away everything in the King's tent. Therefore the King, most worthily, has caused every soldier to cut his prisoner's throat. O, it's a gallant king!
FLUELLEN. Aye, he was born at Monmouth, Captain Gower. What do you call the town where Alexander the Pig was born?
GOWER. Alexander the Great.
FLUELLEN. Why, I pray you, is not "pig" "great"? The pig, or the great, or the mighty, or the huge, or the magnanimous, are all one reckoning, save the phrase is a little variation.
GOWER. I think Alexander the Great was born in Macedon. His father was called Philip of Macedon, as I take it.

FLUELLEN. I think it is in Macedon where Alexander was born. I tell you, Captain, if you look in the maps of the world, I warrant you shall find, in the comparisons between Macedon and Monmouth, that the situations, look you, are both alike. There is a river in Macedon; and there is also moreover a river at Monmouth—it is called the Wye at Monmouth; but it is out of my brain what the name of the other river is. But it is all one, it is alike as my fingers are to my fingers, and there are salmon in both. If you mark Alexander's life well, Harry of Monmouth's life follows after it indifferently well; for there are parallels in all things. Alexander, God knows, and you know, in his rages and his furies and his wraths and his angers and his moods and his displeasures and his indignations, and also being a little intoxicated in his brains, did, in his ales and his angers, look you, kill his best friend, Cleitus.
GOWER. Our King is not like him in that. He never killed any of his friends.

FLUELLEN. It is not well done, mark you now, to take the tale out of my mouth before it is made and finished. I speak only in the figures and comparisons of it. As Alexander killed his friend Cleitus, being in his ales and his cups; so also Harry Monmouth, being in his right wits and his good judgment, turned away the fat knight with the great-bellied doublet. He was full of jests, and gibes, and knaveries, and mocks; I have forgotten his name.
GOWER. Sir John Falstaff.
FLUELLEN. That is he. I'll tell you, there are good men born at Monmouth.
GOWER. Here comes his Majesty.
[Alarum. Enter King Henry and forces; Warwick, Gloucester, Exeter with prisoners. Flourish.]

KING HENRY V. I have not been angry since I came to France until this very moment. Take a trumpet, herald; ride to the horsemen on yonder hill. If they will fight with us, bid them come down—or quit the field; they offend our sight. If they will do neither, we will come to them, and make them scurry away as swift as stones flung from the old Assyrian slings. Besides, we will cut the throats of those we have, and not a man of those we shall take shall taste our mercy. Go and tell them so.
[Enter Montjoy.]
EXETER. Here comes the herald of the French, my liege.
GLOUCESTER. His eyes are humbler than they used to be.
KING HENRY V. How now! What does this mean, herald? Don't you know I have settled these bones of mine for ransom? Have you come again for ransom?

MONTJOY. No, great King; I come to you for charitable permission, that we may go over this bloody field to count our dead, and then bury them; to sort our nobles from our common men. For many of our princes—woe is the time!—lie drowned and soaked in mercenary blood; just as our commoners drench their peasant limbs in the blood of princes. And their wounded steeds prance fetlock-deep in gore, and in wild rage kick out their armored heels at their dead masters, killing them twice. O, give us leave, great King, to view the field in safety, and dispose of their dead bodies!
KING HENRY V. I tell you truly, herald, I do not know whether the day is ours or not; for still many of your horsemen are visible and galloping over the field.
MONTJOY. The day is yours.
KING HENRY V. Praised be God, and not our strength, for it! What is this castle called that stands close by?
MONTJOY. They call it Agincourt.
KING HENRY V. Then we'll call this the field of Agincourt, fought on the day of Crispin Crispianus.

FLUELLEN. Your grandfather of famous memory, if it please your Majesty, and your great-uncle Edward the Black Prince of Wales, as I have read in the chronicles, fought a most brave battle here in France.
KING HENRY V. They did, Fluellen.

FLUELLEN. Your Majesty says very true. If your Majesties remember it, the Welshmen did good service in a garden where leeks did grow, wearing leeks in their Monmouth caps; which, your Majesty knows, to this hour is an honorable badge of that service. And I do believe your Majesty takes no scorn to wear the leek upon Saint David's day.
KING HENRY V. I wear it for a memorable honor; for I am Welsh, you know, good countryman.
FLUELLEN. All the water in the Wye cannot wash your Majesty's Welsh blood out of your body, I can tell you that. God bless it and preserve it, as long as it pleases His grace, and His majesty too!
KING HENRY V. Thanks, my good countryman.

FLUELLEN. By Jesu, I am your Majesty's countryman, I do not care who knows it. I will confess it to all the world. I need not be ashamed of your Majesty, praised be God, so long as your Majesty is an honest man.
KING HENRY V. God keep me so!
[Enter Williams.]
Our heralds go with him; bring me accurate report of the numbers dead on both sides. Call that fellow yonder here.
[Exeunt Heralds with Montjoy.]
EXETER. Soldier, you must come to the King.
KING HENRY V. Soldier, why do you wear that glove in your cap?
WILLIAMS. If it please your Majesty, it is the token of a man I am to fight with, if he is alive.
KING HENRY V. An Englishman?

WILLIAMS. If it please your Majesty, a rascal who swaggered with me last night; who, if alive and ever dares to claim this glove, I have sworn to give him a box on the ear; or if I see my glove in his cap—which he swore, as he was a soldier, he would wear if alive—I will strike it out soundly.
KING HENRY V. What do you think, Captain Fluellen—is it fitting that this soldier keep his oath?
FLUELLEN. He is a coward and a villain otherwise, if it please your Majesty, in my conscience.
KING HENRY V. It may be that his enemy is a gentleman of great rank, quite beyond the reach of his station.

FLUELLEN. Though he be as good a gentleman as the devil is, as Lucifer and Beelzebub himself, it is necessary, look your Grace, that he keep his vow and his oath. If he is forsworn, see you now, his reputation is as outright a villain and a knave-Jack as ever his black shoe trod upon God's ground and His earth, in my conscience, indeed!
KING HENRY V. Then keep your vow, sirrah, when you meet the fellow.
WILLIAMS. So I will, my liege, as I live.
KING HENRY V. Under whom do you serve?
WILLIAMS. Under Captain Gower, my liege.
FLUELLEN. Gower is a good captain, and is good knowledge and literatured in the wars.
KING HENRY V. Call him here to me, soldier.
WILLIAMS. I will, my liege.
[Exit.]

KING HENRY V. Here, Fluellen; wear this favor for me and stick it in your cap. When Alençon and I were down together, I plucked this glove from his helmet. If any man claims this, he is a friend to Alençon, and an enemy to my person. If you encounter any such, arrest him—if you love me.

FLUELLEN. Your Grace does me as great honor as can be wished in the hearts of his subjects. I would gladly see the man, with only two legs, who will find himself aggrieved at this glove; that is all. But I would gladly see it once, if it please God in His grace that I might see.
KING HENRY V. Do you know Gower?
FLUELLEN. He is my dear friend, if it please you.
KING HENRY V. Please, go find him, and bring him to my tent.
FLUELLEN. I will fetch him.
[Exit.]

KING HENRY V. My Lord of Warwick, and my brother Gloucester, follow Fluellen closely at the heels. The glove which I have given him for a favor may perhaps buy him a box on the ear. It is the soldier's; I by our bargain should be wearing it myself. Follow, good cousin Warwick. If the soldier strikes him—as I judge by his blunt bearing he will keep his word—some sudden mischief may arise from it. For I know Fluellen is valiant, and, touched with anger, hot as gunpowder, and will quickly return an injury. Follow, and see there is no harm between them. Come with me, uncle of Exeter.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 8 — Before King Henry’s pavilion
paragraphs: [Enter Gower and Williams.]
WILLIAMS. I warrant it is to knight you, Captain.
[Enter Fluellen.]
FLUELLEN. God's will and his pleasure, captain, I beseech you now, come quickly to the King. There is perhaps more good toward you than is in your knowledge to dream of.
WILLIAMS. Sir, do you know this glove?
FLUELLEN. Know the glove! I know the glove is a glove.
WILLIAMS. I know this; and thus I claim it.
[Strikes him.]
FLUELLEN. 'Sblood! As outright a traitor as any in the universal world, or in France, or in England!
GOWER. How now, sir! You villain!
WILLIAMS. Do you think I'll be forsworn?
FLUELLEN. Stand aside, Captain Gower. I will give treason his payment in blows, I warrant you.
WILLIAMS. I am no traitor.
FLUELLEN. That's a lie in your throat. I charge you, in his Majesty's name, arrest him; he is a friend of the Duke of Alençon's.
[Enter Warwick and Gloucester.]
WARWICK. How now, how now! What's the matter?
FLUELLEN. My lord of Warwick, here is—praised be God for it!—a most contagious treason come to light, look you, as you could wish to find on a summer's day. Here is his Majesty.
[Enter King Henry and Exeter.]
KING HENRY V. How now! What's the matter?
FLUELLEN. My liege, here is a villain and a traitor who, look your Grace, has struck the glove that your Majesty took out of the helmet of Alençon.

WILLIAMS. My liege, this was my glove; here is the fellow to it; and he that I gave it to in exchange promised to wear it in his cap. I promised to strike him if he did. I met this man with my glove in his cap, and I have been as good as my word.

FLUELLEN. Your Majesty hear now, saving your Majesty's manhood, what an outright, rascally, beggarly, lousy knave he is. I hope your Majesty will bear me testimony and witness, and will avouch, that this is the glove of Alençon that your Majesty gave me; in your conscience, now?
KING HENRY V. Give me your glove, soldier. Look, here is its fellow. It was I, indeed, you promised to strike; and you have given me most bitter terms.
FLUELLEN. If it please your Majesty, let his neck answer for it, if there is any martial law in the world.
KING HENRY V. How can you make me satisfaction?
WILLIAMS. All offenses, my lord, come from the heart. Never came any from mine that might offend your Majesty.
KING HENRY V. It was I yourself you did abuse.

WILLIAMS. Your Majesty did not come as yourself. You appeared to me as just a common man—witness the night, your garments, your low manner. And what your Highness suffered under that appearance, I beseech you take as your own fault, not mine. For had you been what I took you for, I made no offense. Therefore, I beseech your Highness, pardon me.

KING HENRY V. Here, uncle Exeter, fill this glove with crowns, and give it to this fellow. Keep it, fellow; and wear it for an honor in your cap until I do claim it. Give him his crowns. And, captain, you must be friends with him.

FLUELLEN. By this day and this light, the fellow has mettle enough in his belly. Here, here is twelve pence for you; and I pray you to serve God, and keep yourself out of brawls, and prabbles, and quarrels, and disputes—and, I warrant you, it is the better for you.
WILLIAMS. I will have none of your money.

FLUELLEN. It is with a good will; I can tell you, it will serve you to mend your shoes. Come, why should you be so bashful? Your shoes are not so good. It is a good shilling, I warrant you, or I will change it.
[Enter an English Herald.]
KING HENRY V. Now, herald—are the dead counted?
HERALD. Here is the number of the slaughtered French.
KING HENRY V. What prisoners of high rank are taken, uncle?
EXETER. Charles Duke of Orleans, nephew to the King; John Duke of Bourbon, and Lord Boucicault. Of other lords and barons, knights and squires—a full fifteen hundred, besides common men.

KING HENRY V. This note tells me of ten thousand French who lie slain in the field. Of princes in this number, and nobles bearing banners, there lie dead one hundred twenty-six. Added to these, of knights, squires, and gallant gentlemen, eight thousand four hundred; of which five hundred were dubbed knights only yesterday. So that, in these ten thousand they have lost, there are only sixteen hundred mercenaries; the rest are princes, barons, lords, knights, squires, and gentlemen of blood and quality. The names of those nobles of theirs who lie dead: Charles Delabreth, High Constable of France; Jacques of Chatillon, Admiral of France; the master of the Crossbows, Lord Rambures; Great Master of France, the brave Sir Guichard Dauphin; John, Duke of Alençon; Anthony, Duke of Brabant, the brother to the Duke of Burgundy; and Edward, Duke of Bar. Of lusty earls: Grandpré and Roussi, Fauconbridge and Foix, Beaumont and Marle, Vaudemont and Lestrale. Here was a royal fellowship of death! Where is the number of our English dead?
[Herald gives him another paper.]

Edward the Duke of York, the Earl of Suffolk, Sir Richard Ketly, Davy Gam, esquire; none else of name. And of all other men, only twenty-five.—O God, your arm was here; and not to us, but to your arm alone, do we ascribe it all! When, without stratagem, but in plain shock and even play of battle, was there ever known so great and so small a loss on one side and on the other? Take it, God, for it is none but yours!
EXETER. It is wonderful!

KING HENRY V. Come, let us go in procession to the village; and let it be proclaimed, under penalty of death throughout our host, that no man boast of this, or take from God that praise which is His only.
FLUELLEN. Is it not lawful, if it please your Majesty, to tell how many were killed?
KING HENRY V. Yes, Captain; but with this acknowledgment—that God fought for us.
FLUELLEN. Yes, my conscience, He did us great good.

KING HENRY V. Let us do all holy rites. Let there be sung _Non nobis_ and _Te Deum_; let the dead be enclosed in clay with charity. And then to Calais; and to England then, where never from France arrived more happy men.
[Exeunt.]
[Enter Chorus.]

CHORUS. Vouchsafe to those who have not read the story, that I may prompt them; and of such as have, I humbly pray them to allow the excuse of time, of numbers, and the due course of things, which cannot in their huge and proper life be presented here. Now we carry the King toward Calais; grant him there; there seen, heave him away upon your winged thoughts across the sea. Behold, the English beach turns pale in the flood with men, with wives, and boys, whose shouts and claps out-voice the deep-mouthed sea, which, like a mighty marshal before the King, seems to prepare his way. So let him land, and solemnly see him set out for London. So swift a pace has thought that even now you may imagine him upon Blackheath, where his lords desire him to have his bruised helmet and his bent sword borne before him through the city. He forbids it, being free from vanity and self-glorious pride; giving the full trophy, sign, and pomp quite away from himself, to God. But now behold, in the quick forge and working-house of thought, how London pours out her citizens! The mayor and all his brethren in their best attire, like the senators of ancient Rome, with the plebeians swarming at their heels, go forth and fetch their conquering Caesar in—as, by a lower but loving likelihood, were now the general of our gracious empress (as in good time he may), coming from Ireland, bringing rebellion impaled on his sword: how many would quit the peaceful city to welcome him! Much more, and with much more cause, did they this Harry. Now place him in London; for now the lamentation of the French invites the King of England's stay at home—the Emperor's coming on behalf of France to order peace between them—and we shall pass over all the events, whatever happened, until Harry's return again to France. There we must bring him; and I myself have played the interim, by reminding you it is past. Then accept this abridgement, and let your eyes advance after your thoughts, straight back again to France.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — France. The English camp
paragraphs: [Enter Fluellen and Gower.]
GOWER. No, that's right; but why are you wearing your leek today? Saint David's day is past.

FLUELLEN. There are occasions and causes why and wherefore in all things. I will tell you as my friend, Captain Gower. The rascally, scabby, beggarly, lousy, bragging knave Pistol—whom you and yourself and all the world know to be no better than a fellow, look you now, of no merits—he came to me yesterday and brought me bread and salt, look you, and told me to eat my leek. It was in a place where I could not raise a quarrel with him; but I will be so bold as to wear it in my cap till I see him once again, and then I will tell him a little piece of my mind.
[Enter Pistol.]
GOWER. Why, here he comes, swelling like a turkey cock.
FLUELLEN. It is no matter for his swellings or his turkey-cocks. God bless you, Ensign Pistol! You scurvy, lousy knave, God bless you!
PISTOL. Ha! Are you mad? Do you thirst, base Trojan, to have me fold up Fate's fatal web? Begone! I am queasy at the smell of leek.

FLUELLEN. I beseech you heartily, scurvy, lousy knave, at my desires, and my requests, and my petitions, to eat, look you, this leek. Because, look you, you do not love it, nor your affections and your appetites and your digestions do not agree with it, I would desire you to eat it.
PISTOL. Not for Cadwallader and all his goats.
FLUELLEN. There is one goat for you. [Strikes him.] Will you be so good, scabby knave, as to eat it?
PISTOL. Base Trojan, you shall die.

FLUELLEN. You say very true, scabby knave, when God's will is. I will ask you to live in the meantime, and eat your food. Come, there is sauce for it. [Strikes him.] You called me "mountain-squire" yesterday; but I will make you today a squire of low degree. I pray you, fall to; if you can mock a leek, you can eat a leek.
GOWER. Enough, captain; you have astonished him.
FLUELLEN. I say, I will make him eat some part of my leek, or I will beat his head for four days. Bite, I pray you; it is good for your green wound and your bloody coxcomb.
PISTOL. Must I bite?
FLUELLEN. Yes, certainly, and out of doubt and out of question too, and ambiguities.
PISTOL. By this leek, I will most horribly revenge. I eat and eat, I swear—
FLUELLEN. Eat, I pray you. Will you have some more sauce to your leek? There is not enough leek to swear by.
PISTOL. Quiet your cudgel; you do see I eat.

FLUELLEN. Much good may it do you, scabby knave, heartily. No, please, throw none away—the skin is good for your broken coxcomb. When you take occasions to see leeks hereafter, I pray you, mock at them; that is all.
PISTOL. Good.
FLUELLEN. Aye, leeks are good. Here, here is a groat to heal your head.
PISTOL. A groat for me!
FLUELLEN. Yes, truly and in truth you shall take it; or I have another leek in my pocket, which you shall eat.
PISTOL. I take your groat as down payment on revenge.
FLUELLEN. If I owe you anything I will pay you in cudgels. You shall be a wood-monger, and buy nothing of me but cudgels. God be with you, and keep you, and heal your head.
[Exit.]
PISTOL. All hell shall stir for this.

GOWER. Go, go; you are a counterfeit cowardly knave. Will you mock at an ancient tradition, begun upon an honorable basis, and worn as a memorable trophy of long-dead valor, and dare not back up in your deeds any of your words? I have seen you mocking and galling at this gentleman two or three times. You thought, because he could not speak English in the native style, he could not therefore handle an English cudgel. You find it otherwise; and henceforth let a Welsh correction teach you a good English manner. Fare you well.
[Exit.]

PISTOL. Does Fortune play the housewife with me now? News have I that my Doll is dead in the hospital of the French disease; and there my home rendezvous is quite cut off. Old I do grow; and from my weary limbs honor is cudgeled out. Well, I'll turn pimp, and lean a little toward cutpurse of quick hand. To England I will steal, and there I'll steal; and bandages I will get for these cudgeled scars, and swear I got them in the wars of France.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — France. A royal palace
paragraphs: [Enter at one door, King Henry, Exeter, Bedford, Warwick, Gloucester, Westmorland, Clarence, Huntingdon and other Lords. At another, Queen Isabel, the French King, the Princess Katherine, Alice, and other Ladies; the Duke of Burgundy and other French.]

KING HENRY V. Peace to this meeting, which is the reason we are met! To our brother France, and to our sister, health and fair time of day; joy and good wishes to our most fair and princely cousin Katherine. And, as a branch and member of this royalty, by whom this great assembly has been arranged, we salute you, Duke of Burgundy. And, princes French, and peers, health to you all!
FRENCH KING. Right joyous are we to behold your face, most worthy brother England; fairly met! So are you, princes English, every one.

QUEEN ISABEL. So happy be the outcome, brother England, of this good day and of this gracious meeting, as we are now glad to behold your eyes—your eyes, which until now have carried in them, against the Frenchmen who met their gaze, the fatal balls of murdering basilisks. The venom of such looks, we fairly hope, has lost its power; and this day shall change all griefs and quarrels into love.
KING HENRY V. To cry amen to that, we are here.
QUEEN ISABEL. You English princes all, I salute you.

BURGUNDY. My duty to you both, in equal love, great Kings of France and England! That I have labored, with all my wits, my pains, and my strong endeavors, to bring your most imperial Majesties to this bar and royal interview—your mightiness on both sides can best witness. Since then my office has so far prevailed that, face to face and royal eye to eye, you have greeted one another, let it not disgrace me if I demand, before this royal view, what obstacle or what impediment there is why the naked, poor, and mangled Peace, dear nurse of arts, plenty, and joyful births, should not in this best garden of the world, our fertile France, put up her lovely face? Alas, she has too long been chased from France, and all her husbandry lies in heaps, corrupting in its own fertility. Her vine, the merry cheerer of the heart, unpruned dies; her hedges, once evenly woven, like prisoners wildly overgrown with hair, put forth disordered twigs; her fallow fields the darnel, hemlock, and rank fumitory take root upon, while the plow-blade rusts that should uproot such savagery. The even meadow, that once brought sweetly forth the freckled cowslip, burnet, and green clover, lacking the scythe, all uncorrected, rank, conceives by idleness, and bears nothing but hateful docks, rough thistles, dry stalks, burs, losing both beauty and usefulness. And as our vineyards, fallow fields, meadows, and hedges, defective in their natures, grow to wildness—even so our houses and ourselves and children have lost, or do not learn for lack of time, the sciences that should beautify our country, but grow like savages—as soldiers will, who do nothing but meditate on blood—to swearing and stern looks, slovenly attire, and everything that seems unnatural. To restore which to our former condition you are assembled; and my speech entreats that I may know the obstacle, why gentle Peace should not expel these inconveniences and bless us with her former qualities.

KING HENRY V. If, Duke of Burgundy, you would have the peace, whose absence gives growth to the imperfections you have cited, you must buy that peace with full accord to all our just demands. Their substance and particular effects you have briefly listed in your hands.
BURGUNDY. The King has heard them; to which as yet no answer has been made.
KING HENRY V. Well then, the peace which you before so urged lies in his answer.

FRENCH KING. I have only with a hasty eye glanced over the articles. If it pleases your Grace to appoint some of your council presently to sit with us once more, with better attention to re-examine them, we will quickly give our final and binding answer.

KING HENRY V. Brother, we shall. Go, uncle Exeter, and brother Clarence, and you, brother Gloucester, Warwick, and Huntington—go with the King. And take with you full power to ratify, augment, or alter, as your wisdom best shall see advantageous for our dignity, anything in or out of our demands, and we'll agree to it. Will you, fair sister, go with the princes, or stay here with us?
QUEEN ISABEL. Our gracious brother, I will go with them. Perhaps a woman's voice may do some good, when articles too nicely urged are stood upon.
KING HENRY V. Yet leave our cousin Katherine here with us. She is our chief demand, set in the front rank of our articles.
QUEEN ISABEL. She has good leave.
[Exeunt all except Henry, Katherine and Alice.]
KING HENRY V. Fair Katherine, and most fair, will you vouchsafe to teach a soldier terms such as will enter a lady's ear and plead his love-suit to her gentle heart?
KATHERINE. Your Majesty shall mock me; I cannot speak your England.
KING HENRY V. O fair Katherine, if you will love me soundly with your French heart, I will be glad to hear you confess it brokenly with your English tongue. Do you like me, Kate?
KATHERINE. _Pardonnez-moi_, I cannot tell what is "like me."
KING HENRY V. An angel is like you, Kate, and you are like an angel.
KATHERINE. _Que dit-il? Que je suis semblable à les anges?_—What does he say? That I am like the angels?
ALICE. _Oui, vraiment, sauf votre Grâce, ainsi dit-il._—Yes, truly, saving your Grace, so he says.
KING HENRY V. I said so, dear Katherine; and I must not blush to affirm it.
KATHERINE. _O bon Dieu! les langues des hommes sont pleines de tromperies._—O good God! The tongues of men are full of deceits.
KING HENRY V. What does she say, fair one? That the tongues of men are full of deceits?
ALICE. _Oui_, that the tongues of the men is be full of deceits: that is the Princess.

KING HENRY V. The Princess is the better Englishwoman. I'faith, Kate, my wooing is fit for your understanding. I am glad you can speak no better English; for if you could, you would find me such a plain king that you would think I had sold my farm to buy my crown. I know no ways to mince it in love—but directly to say, "I love you." Then if you urge me further than to say, "Do you, in faith?" I run out of suit. Give me your answer; i'faith, do; and so clap hands and a bargain. How say you, lady?
KATHERINE. _Sauf votre honneur_, me understand well.

KING HENRY V. By Mary, if you would put me to verses, or to dance for your sake, Kate, why, you'd undo me. For the one, I have neither words nor measure; and for the other I have no strength in the measure—yet a reasonable measure in strength. If I could win a lady at leapfrog, or by vaulting into my saddle with my armor on my back, under the correction of bragging be it spoken, I should quickly leap into a wife. Or if I might box for my love, or curvet my horse for her favors, I could lay on like a butcher and sit like a jackanapes, never off. But before God, Kate, I cannot look bashful, nor gasp out my eloquence, nor have I any cunning in protestation—only downright oaths, which I never use till urged, nor ever break by being urged. If you can love a fellow of this temper, Kate, whose face is not worth sunburning, who never looks in his mirror for love of anything he sees there, let your eye be your cook. I speak to you as a plain soldier. If you can love me for this, take me; if not, to tell you that I shall die is true; but for your love, by the Lord, no—yet I love you too. And while you live, dear Kate, take a fellow of plain and uncoined constancy; for he must of necessity do you right, because he has not the gift to woo in other places. For these fellows of infinite tongue, who can rhyme themselves into ladies' favors, they always reason themselves out again. What! A speaker is only a prattler; a rhyme is only a ballad. A good leg will fail; a straight back will stoop; a black beard will turn white; a curly head will grow bald; a fair face will wither; a full eye will go hollow. But a good heart, Kate, is the sun and the moon—or rather the sun, and not the moon; for it shines bright and never changes, but keeps its course truly. If you would have such a one, take me; and take me, take a soldier; take a soldier, take a king. And what do you say then to my love? Speak, my fair, and fairly, I pray you.
KATHERINE. Is it possible that I should love the enemy of France?

KING HENRY V. No; it is not possible you should love the enemy of France, Kate; but in loving me, you would love the friend of France. For I love France so well that I will not part with a village of it; I will have it all mine. And, Kate, when France is mine and I am yours, then yours is France and you are mine.
KATHERINE. I cannot tell what is that.

KING HENRY V. No, Kate? I will tell you in French—which I am sure will hang upon my tongue like a new-married wife around her husband's neck, hardly to be shaken off. _Je quand sur le possession de France, et quand vous avez le possession de moi_—let me see, what then? Saint Denis be my speed!—_donc votre est France, et vous êtes mienne._ It is as easy for me, Kate, to conquer the kingdom as to speak so much more French. I shall never move you in French, unless it be to laugh at me.
KATHERINE. _Sauf votre honneur, le français que vous parlez, il est meilleur que l'anglais lequel je parle._—Saving your honor, the French you speak is better than the English I speak.

KING HENRY V. No, faith, it is not, Kate; but your speaking of my tongue, and I of yours, most truly-falsely, must needs be granted to be much the same. But, Kate, do you understand this much English: can you love me?
KATHERINE. I cannot tell.

KING HENRY V. Can any of your neighbors tell, Kate? I'll ask them. Come, I know you love me; and at night, when you come into your closet, you'll question this gentlewoman about me; and I know, Kate, you will, to her, dispraise those parts in me that you love with your heart. But, good Kate, mock me mercifully—the rather, gentle princess, because I love you cruelly. If ever you are mine, Kate—as I have a saving faith within me which tells me you shall—I get you with scrambling, and you must therefore prove a good soldier-breeder. Shall not you and I, between Saint Denis and Saint George, compound a boy, half French, half English, that shall go to Constantinople and take the Turk by the beard? Shall we not? What do you say, my fair fleur-de-lis?
KATHERINE. I do not know that.

KING HENRY V. No; it is hereafter to know, but now to promise. Just promise now, Kate, that you will endeavor for your French part of such a boy; and for my English half, take the word of a king and a bachelor. How do you answer, _la plus belle Katherine du monde, mon très cher et divin déesse?_—the most beautiful Katherine in the world, my very dear and divine goddess?
KATHERINE. Your Majesty have _fausse_—false—French enough to deceive the most _sage demoiselle_—wise young lady—that is _en France_—in France.

KING HENRY V. Now, fie upon my false French! By my honor, in true English, I love you, Kate. By which honor I dare not swear that you love me; yet my blood begins to flatter me that you do, despite the poor and untempting effect of my face. Now, curse my father's ambition! He was thinking of civil wars when he begot me; and so I was created with a stubborn outside, with an iron aspect, that when I come to woo ladies, I frighten them. But, in faith, Kate, the older I grow, the better I shall appear. My comfort is that old age, that ill keeper of beauty, can do no more damage to my face. You have me, if you have me, at the worst; and you shall wear me, if you wear me, better and better. And therefore tell me, most fair Katherine, will you have me? Put off your maiden blushes; avouch the thoughts of your heart with the looks of an empress; take me by the hand, and say, "Harry of England, I am yours." Which word you shall no sooner bless my ear with than I will tell you aloud: England is yours, Ireland is yours, France is yours, and Henry Plantagenet is yours; who, though I speak it before his face, if he is not fellow with the best king, you shall find the best king of good fellows. Come, your answer in broken music—for your voice is music and your English broken; therefore, queen of all, Katherine, break your mind to me in broken English. Will you have me?
KATHERINE. That is as it shall please _le roi mon père_—the king my father.
KING HENRY V. No, it will please him well, Kate; it shall please him, Kate.
KATHERINE. Then it shall also content me.
KING HENRY V. Upon that I kiss your hand, and call you my queen.

KATHERINE. _Laissez, mon seigneur, laissez, laissez! Ma foi, je ne veux point que vous abaissiez votre grandeur en baisant la main d'une—Notre Seigneur!—indigne serviteur. Excusez-moi, je vous supplie, mon très-puissant seigneur._—Leave off, my lord, leave off! By my faith, I do not want you to lower your greatness by kissing the hand of one—Our Lord!—unworthy servant. Excuse me, I beg you, my most powerful lord.
KING HENRY V. Then I will kiss your lips, Kate.

KATHERINE. _Les dames et demoiselles pour être baisées devant leurs noces, il n'est pas la coutume de France._—For ladies and young women to be kissed before their weddings, it is not the custom of France.
KING HENRY V. Madame my interpreter, what does she say?
ALICE. That it is not the fashion _pour les_—for the—ladies of France—I cannot tell what is _baiser en_ English.
KING HENRY V. To kiss.
ALICE. Your Majesty _entend_—understand—better _que moi_—than I.
KING HENRY V. It is not the fashion for the maids in France to kiss before they are married, would she say?
ALICE. _Oui, vraiment._—Yes, truly.

KING HENRY V. O Kate, nice customs curtsy to great kings. Dear Kate, you and I cannot be confined within the weak boundary of a country's fashion. We are the makers of manners, Kate; and the liberty that follows our station stops the mouth of all fault-finders, as I will do to yours, for upholding the nice fashion of your country in denying me a kiss. Therefore, patiently and yielding. [Kissing her.] You have witchcraft in your lips, Kate; there is more eloquence in a sugar-sweet touch of them than in the tongues of the French council; and they would sooner persuade Harry of England than a general petition from all the monarchs. Here comes your father.
[Enter the French Power and the English Lords.]
BURGUNDY. God save your Majesty! My royal cousin, do you teach our princess English?
KING HENRY V. I would have her learn, my fair cousin, how perfectly I love her; and that is good English.
BURGUNDY. Is she not apt?

KING HENRY V. Our tongue is rough, cousin, and my manner is not smooth—so that, having neither the voice nor the heart of flattery about me, I cannot so conjure up the spirit of love in her, that he will appear in his true likeness.

BURGUNDY. Pardon the frankness of my mirth, if I answer you for that. If you would conjure in her, you must make a circle; if conjure up Love in her in his true likeness, he must appear naked and blind. Can you blame her then, being a maid yet rose-colored with the virgin crimson of modesty, if she denies the appearance of a naked blind boy in her naked seeing self? It would be, my lord, a hard condition for a maid to agree to.
KING HENRY V. Yet they do close their eyes and yield, since love is blind and forces them.
BURGUNDY. They are then excused, my lord, when they see not what they do.
KING HENRY V. Then, good my lord, teach your cousin to consent with her eyes shut.

BURGUNDY. I will wink at her to consent, my lord, if you will teach her to understand my meaning. For maids, well summered and warmly kept, are like flies at Bartholomew-tide—blind, though they have their eyes; and then they will endure handling, which before would not abide looking on.
KING HENRY V. This moral ties me over to wait for time and a hot summer. And so I shall catch the fly, your cousin, at the latter end—and she must be blind too.
BURGUNDY. As love is, my lord, before it loves.
KING HENRY V. It is so; and some of you may thank love for my blindness, who cannot see many a fair French city for one fair French maid that stands in my way.
FRENCH KING. Yes, my lord, you see them in perspective: the cities turned into a maid; for they are all girdled with maiden walls that no war has entered.
KING HENRY V. Shall Kate be my wife?
FRENCH KING. So please you.
KING HENRY V. I am content, so the maiden cities you talk of may attend on her; so the maid who stood in the way of my wish shall show me the way to my will.
FRENCH KING. We have consented to all reasonable terms.
KING HENRY V. Is that so, my lords of England?
WESTMORLAND. The King has granted every article: his daughter first, and then in sequence all, according to their firm proposed natures.

EXETER. Only he has not yet subscribed to this: where your Majesty demands that the King of France, having any occasion to write for matter of grant, shall name your Highness in this form and with this addition, in French: _Notre très-cher fils Henri, Roi d'Angleterre, Héritier de France_—Our very dear son Henry, King of England, Heir of France—and thus in Latin, _Praeclarissimus filius noster Henricus, rex Angliae et haeres Franciae._
FRENCH KING. Nor have I, brother, so denied this article that I will not let it pass at your request.
KING HENRY V. I pray you then, in love and dear alliance, let that one article rank with the rest; and thereupon give me your daughter.

FRENCH KING. Take her, fair son, and from her blood raise up issue to me, that the contending kingdoms of France and England, whose very shores look pale with envy of each other's happiness, may cease their hatred; and this dear conjunction plant neighborliness and Christian-like accord in their sweet bosoms, so that never may war advance his bleeding sword between England and fair France.
LORDS. Amen!
KING HENRY V. Now, welcome, Kate; and bear me witness all, that here I kiss her as my sovereign queen.
[Flourish.]

QUEEN ISABEL. God, the best maker of all marriages, combine your hearts in one, your realms in one! As man and wife, being two, are one in love, so be there between your kingdoms such a spousal that never may ill office or fell jealousy, which troubles often the bed of blessed marriage, thrust in between the pact of these kingdoms to make divorce of their incorporate league—so that English may, as French, and French Englishmen, receive each other. God speak this Amen!
ALL. Amen!

KING HENRY V. Let us prepare for our marriage; on which day, my Lord of Burgundy, we'll take your oath, and all the peers', for surety of our leagues. Then shall I swear to Kate, and you to me; and may our oaths be well kept and prosperous!
[Sennet. Exeunt.]
EPILOGUE.
[Enter Chorus.]

CHORUS. Thus far, with rough and unequal pen, our bowing author has pursued the story, in a little room confining mighty men, mangling by starts the full course of their glory. Small time, but in that small most greatly lived this star of England. Fortune made his sword, by which the world's best garden he achieved, and of it left his son imperial lord. Henry the Sixth, in infant bands crowned King of France and England, succeeded this king. His state so many had the managing of, that they lost France and made his England bleed—which often our stage has shown; and, for their sake, in your fair minds let this acceptance take.
[Exit.]
